div.p: While there are many matters in philosophy that even now have by no means been adequately explained, the inquiry into the nature of the gods is one of peculiar difficulty and obscurity, as you, Brutus, are very well aware — an inquiry which is at once the noblest of all for the understanding of the mind and indispensable for the regulation of religion. On this subject the opinions of the most learned men are so various and so much at odds with one another that this very fact ought to be taken as strong evidence that the starting-point of philosophy lies in our want of knowledge, and that the Academics have shown good sense in withholding assent from things uncertain. For what is more shameful than rashness, and what is so reckless and so unworthy of the gravity and steadfastness of the wise man as either to hold a false opinion, or to defend without the least hesitation something that has not been grasped and understood with sufficient certainty?

When Cotta had thus spoken, Velleius said: "How rash of me, to have ventured to engage with an Academic who is at the same time a rhetorician! For an Academic without eloquence I should not have greatly dreaded, nor a rhetorician, however eloquent, without that philosophy; for I am not confounded by a flood of empty words, nor by subtlety of thought if the speech is dry. But you, Cotta, were strong in both respects; only the ring of bystanders and the jury were wanting to you. But of that another time; now let us hear Lucilius, if it suits him."

When Balbus had thus spoken, Cotta said with a smile: "Too late, Balbus, do you instruct me what to defend. For while you were arguing I was myself pondering what I should say against you — not so much for the sake of refuting you as of asking about the things I understood less well. But since each man must use his own judgement, it is hard for me to think as you would wish."

In the present inquiry, for instance, most thinkers have affirmed the existence of the gods — which is most likely to be true, and to which we are all led by the guidance of Nature herself; but Protagoras declared himself in doubt, while Diagoras of Melos and Theodorus of Cyrene held that there are no gods at all. As for those who have affirmed that the gods exist, they differ so widely and disagree so much that it would be an endless task to enumerate their opinions. Much is said about the shapes of the gods, about their dwelling-places and abodes, and about the manner of their life, and on these points the philosophers wrangle in the bitterest disagreement. But the question that most truly contains the heart of the matter is this: whether the gods do nothing, set nothing in motion, and stand wholly aloof from all care and administration of things; or whether, on the contrary, all things were made and ordained by them from the beginning and are ruled and moved by them for endless time. On this point above all there is great disagreement, and unless it is decided men must inevitably remain in the deepest error and in ignorance of matters of the highest importance.

Then said Balbus: "For my part I would rather hear Cotta again, so that with the same eloquence with which he abolished the false gods he might bring in the true. For it befits a philosopher, a pontiff, and Cotta to hold about the immortal gods an opinion not wandering and unsettled, as the Academics do, but, as we Stoics do, firm and certain. For against Epicurus enough and more than enough has been said; but I am eager to hear what you yourself, Cotta, think." "Have you forgotten," he said, "what I said at the outset — that I can more easily say, especially on matters of this kind, what I do not think than what I do? And even if I had something clear to offer, I should still wish to hear you in my turn, now that I myself have said so much."

Here Velleius said: "You do not know, Cotta, with what great expectation I shall hear you. For your discourse against Epicurus was pleasing to our Balbus; I therefore in my turn will show myself an attentive hearer of you against the Stoics. For I trust you come, as is your wont, well prepared."

For there are, and have been, philosophers who hold that the gods take no thought whatever for human affairs. If their opinion is true, what room is there for piety, for holiness, for religion? All these are duties to be rendered to the divine power of the gods purely and reverently only on the supposition that the gods take notice of them, and that something has been bestowed upon the human race by the immortal gods. But if the gods can neither help us nor wish to, if they take no care for us at all and pay no heed to what we do, and if nothing can flow from them into the life of men — then what reason is there to offer the immortal gods any worship, honours, or prayers? Piety, like the other virtues, cannot exist in a mere show of feigned pretence; and with piety holiness and religion must likewise be done away, and once these are gone there follows a confounding of life and great confusion.

Then said Balbus: "I will gratify you, and will be as brief as I can; for, the errors of Epicurus refuted, my argument has been relieved of a long discourse. Our school, on the whole, divides this whole question of the immortal gods into four parts. First they teach that the gods exist; next, of what kind they are; then, that the world is administered by them; lastly, that they take thought for human affairs. In this discourse let us take up the first two of these; the third and fourth, being weightier, I think should be put off to another time." "By no means," said Cotta; "for we are at leisure, and we are dealing with matters that are even to be set before our other concerns."

Then said Cotta: "So, by Hercules, I do, Velleius; for my reckoning with Lucilius is not the same as it was with you." "How so, pray?" said he. "Because your Epicurus seems to me not to contend very strongly about the immortal gods: he only does not dare to deny that the gods exist, lest he incur some odium or charge; but when he affirms that the gods do nothing and care for nothing, and that they are endowed with human limbs but have no use of those limbs, he seems to be jesting, and to think it enough if he has said that there is a certain blessed and eternal nature.

And I am inclined to think that, with piety toward the gods removed, good faith too, and the fellowship of the human race, and that most excellent of virtues, justice, are taken away. There are, however, other philosophers, and these great and noble men, who hold that the whole universe is administered and governed by the mind and reason of the gods; and not only this, but that the gods also take counsel and provide for the life of men. For they think that the fruits of the earth and all else that the earth brings forth, the seasons, the changing weather, and the alterations of the sky by which all that the earth produces is ripened and matured, are bestowed by the immortal gods upon the human race; and they gather many proofs, which will be set forth in these books, of a kind that make it seem the immortal gods themselves fashioned these things for the use of men. Against them Carneades argued at such length as to rouse men of any energy to a desire for discovering the truth.

Then said Lucilius: "The first part does not even seem to need a discourse. For what can be so plain and so manifest, when we have looked up at the sky and contemplated the heavens, as that there is some divinity of a most excellent mind by which these things are governed? Were it not so, how could Ennius have said, with the assent of all, 'Behold this gleaming vault on high, whom all men call upon as Jove' — and that very god both Jove, and lord of all things, and ruler of all by his motion, and, as the same Ennius says, 'the father of gods and men,' a god present and all-powerful? And he who doubts this — I really do not see why he might not as well doubt whether there is a sun or none;

But from Balbus you observed, I believe, how many things were said, and how, even if less true, yet apt and coherent among themselves. And so I purpose, as I said, not so much to refute his discourse as to ask about the things I understood less well. Wherefore, Balbus, I leave it to you: would you rather answer me as I ask you about single matters those things which I have grasped too little, or hear my whole discourse through?" Then said Balbus: "For my part, if you wish anything explained to you, I would rather answer; but if you would question me not so much for the sake of understanding as of refuting, I will do as you will, and either answer at once to the several points you ask, or, when you have made your speech, to all."

For there is no subject on which not only the unlearned but even the learned disagree so much; and since their opinions are so various and so much at variance with one another, it may well be that none of them is true, while it is certainly impossible that more than one should be true. Now in this matter we may both appease the well-meaning who reproach us and confute the envious who revile us, so that the latter may repent of their censure while the former may rejoice to have learned something. For those who admonish in a friendly spirit must be instructed, while those who attack in enmity must be repelled.

for what is more evident than the one than the other? And unless we held this fixed and grasped in our minds, so steadfast an opinion would not have endured, nor been confirmed by length of time, nor been able to grow old along with the ages and generations of men. For we see that other opinions, false and empty, have wasted away with time. Who now thinks that the Hippocentaur ever existed, or the Chimaera? What old woman is found so witless as to dread those monsters once believed in among the dead? For time blots out the fictions of opinion, but confirms the judgements of Nature.

Then said Cotta: "Excellent; wherefore let us proceed as the discourse itself leads us. But before the matter, a few words about myself. For I am moved not a little by your authority, Balbus, and by that speech with which, in your peroration, you exhorted me to remember that I am both a Cotta and a pontiff; which, I believe, was meant to this end, that I should defend the opinions about the immortal gods which we have received from our forefathers, and the sacred rites, ceremonies, and observances of religion. These indeed I shall always defend, and always have defended, nor shall the discourse of any man, learned or unlearned, ever move me from that opinion about the worship of the immortal gods which I received from my forefathers. But when it is a question of religion, I follow Tiberius Coruncanius, Publius Scipio, Publius Scaevola, the chief pontiffs, not Zeno or Cleanthes or Chrysippus; and I have Gaius Laelius, an augur and at the same time a wise man, whom I would rather hear speaking of religion in that noble speech of his than any chief of the Stoics. And since the whole religion of the Roman people is divided into rites and auspices, with a third thing joined to these, if from portents and prodigies the interpreters of the Sibyl or the soothsayers have given warning for the sake of prediction, I have judged that none of these religious observances is ever to be despised, and have so persuaded myself that Romulus by the auspices and Numa by the establishment of the rites laid the foundations of our state, which assuredly could never have been so great without the highest favour of the immortal gods.

I notice that much has been said about the books I have lately published in quick succession, and various has been the talk: some wondering whence this sudden zeal for philosophy had sprung up in me; others eager to know what definite views I held on each subject. To many, too, I have observed it seemed strange that I of all men should have given my approval to that philosophy which snatches away the light and pours a kind of night over things, and that I had unexpectedly taken up the defence of a school that had been abandoned and long since deserted. But in fact I did not begin to philosophise on a sudden, nor have I bestowed from my earliest years anything less than great labour and care upon this study; and it was precisely when I seemed least engaged in it that I was most a philosopher — as is shown both by my speeches, which are full of the maxims of philosophers, and by my intimacy with the most learned men, in whom my house has always abounded, and by my having been trained by those eminent teachers, Diodotus, Philo, Antiochus, and Posidonius.

And so, both among our own people and among others, the worship of the gods and the sanctities of religion grow daily greater and better; and this comes about neither by chance nor at random, but because the gods often manifest their power by their presence, as at Lake Regillus in the war with the Latins, when the dictator Aulus Postumius was fighting Octavius Mamilius of Tusculum, Castor and Pollux were seen fighting on horseback in our line; and within more recent memory the same sons of Tyndareus announced the defeat of Perseus. For Publius Vatinius, the grandfather of this youth, as he was coming to Rome by night from the prefecture of Reate, was told by two young men with white horses that king Perseus had that day been captured; and when he reported this to the senate, he was at first thrown into prison, as having spoken too rashly of public affairs, but afterwards, when letters arrived from Paulus and the same day was found to agree, he was rewarded by the senate with land and exemption from service. And again, when the Locrians had overcome the men of Croton in a great battle at the river Sagra, it is recorded that on that very day the news of that fight was heard at the Olympic games. Often the voices of the Fauns have been heard, often the forms of the gods seen, such as to compel any man not dull or impious to confess that the gods are present.

You have, Balbus, what Cotta, what a pontiff thinks; now make me understand what you think; for from you, a philosopher, I ought to receive a reasoned account of religion, but our forefathers I must believe even though no reason is rendered." Then said Balbus: "What reasoned account, then, do you require of me, Cotta?" And he said: "Your division was fourfold: first, that you would teach that the gods exist; next, of what kind they are; then, that the world is ruled by them; lastly, that they take thought for human affairs. This, if I rightly remember, was the partition." "Most rightly," said Balbus; "but I await what you require."

And since all the precepts of philosophy are referred to the conduct of life, I think that both in public and in private affairs I have performed what reason and learning prescribe. But if anyone asks what cause has impelled me to commit these matters to writing so late in life, there is nothing I can more easily explain. For when I was languishing in idleness, and the condition of the commonwealth was such that it had necessarily to be governed by the deliberation and care of one man, I judged that, for the sake of the commonwealth itself, philosophy ought to be expounded to my countrymen, thinking it greatly to the honour and renown of the state that matters so weighty and so noble should be enshrined in Latin letters as well.

As for the predictions and forewarnings of things to come, what else do they declare but that to men the things which are to be are shown, displayed, portended, and foretold? Whence those things are called omens (ostenta), prodigies (monstra), portents (portenta), and signs (prodigia). And if we think those figures the inventions of fabling licence — Mopsus, Tiresias, Amphiaraus, Calchas, Helenus (whom, however, not even the fables would have made augurs if the thing were wholly to be rejected) — shall we not, taught by examples even from our own house, prove the divinity of the gods? Will the rashness of Publius Clodius in the first Punic War not move us at all — who, mocking the gods even in jest, when the chickens, let out of the coop, would not feed, bade them be plunged into the water, that they might drink, since they would not eat? — a jest which, when his fleet was defeated, brought many tears to himself and a great disaster to the Roman people. Did not his colleague Lucius Junius in the same war lose his fleet in a storm because he had not obeyed the auspices? And so Clodius was condemned by the people, and Junius took his own life.

Then said Cotta: "Let us look at each point in turn. And if the first is this, which is agreed among all but the utterly impious, and which indeed cannot be burned out of my mind — that the gods exist — yet of this very thing, of which I am persuaded by the authority of my forefathers, you teach me nothing as to why it is so." "What is it," said Balbus, "if you are persuaded, that you should wish to learn from me?" Then said Cotta: "Because I approach this discussion as though I had never heard anything of the immortal gods, never thought anything; receive me as a raw and untaught pupil, and teach me the things I ask."

And I am the less sorry for my undertaking in that I readily perceive how many I have stirred to a zeal not only for learning but also for writing. For many who had been schooled in Greek teaching were unable to share with their fellow-citizens what they had learned, distrusting whether what they had received from the Greeks could be expressed in Latin; and in this respect we seem to have made such progress that we are not surpassed by the Greeks even in richness of vocabulary.

Coelius writes that Gaius Flaminius, having neglected religion, fell at Trasimene with a great wound to the commonwealth. From whose destruction it may be understood that the commonwealth was enlarged by the commands of those who had obeyed religion. And if we are willing to compare our own affairs with those of foreigners, we shall be found in other respects either equal or even inferior, but in religion — that is, in the worship of the gods — far superior.

"Say, then," said he, "what you ask." "I? — this first: why, when you had said that on this head the matter was so manifest that it did not even need a discourse, because it was manifest and agreed among all that the gods exist, you yet said so many things about that very point." "Because I observed," said he, "that you too, Cotta, often, when you were pleading in the forum, loaded the juror with as many arguments as you could, if only the case gave you the opportunity. And this same thing the philosophers do, and I have done as I could. But what you ask is as if you should ask me why I look at you with two eyes and do not close one, when I could attain the same with one." Then said Cotta: "How like that is, you shall see.

I was urged to turn to these studies also by a sickness of mind brought on by the great and grievous wrong that fortune had done me; and had I been able to find any greater relief from it, I should not have taken refuge in this above all. Yet I could enjoy that very relief in no better way than by devoting myself not merely to the reading of books but to the handling of the whole of philosophy. And all its parts and members are most easily come to know when whole questions are unfolded in writing; for there is a marvellous continuity and connection among things, so that one seems linked to another, and all bound and fastened together.

Or is that augur's staff of Attus Navius, with which he marked out the regions of the vineyard to track down the pig, to be despised? I should believe it, were it not that, on his augury, King Hostilius waged great wars. But through the negligence of the nobility the discipline of augury has been let go, the truth of the auspices despised, and only the form retained; and so the greatest affairs of the commonwealth — among them the wars on which the safety of the commonwealth depends — are managed with no auspices: no watching of the river-crossings, none from the points of the spears, no men summoned to arms (whence in old time wills were made in battle-array); for now our generals begin to wage wars only when they have laid the auspices aside.

For I am not wont, in pleadings, if anything is evident on which all agree, to argue it (for clearness is weakened by argument); nor, if I did it in forensic cases, should I do the same in this fineness of discourse. But there would be no reason for closing one eye, since the gaze of both is the same, and since the nature of things, which you would have to be wise, willed us to have two lights bored through from the mind to the eyes. But because you did not trust that this was as manifest as you wished, for that reason you wished to teach by many arguments that the gods exist. For me one was enough, that our forefathers had so handed it down. But you despise authorities, you fight with reason;

Those who ask what I myself think on each subject are more inquisitive than they need be; for in argument it is not so much the weight of authority as the force of reason that ought to be sought. Indeed the authority of those who profess to teach is generally a hindrance to those who wish to learn; for they cease to use their own judgement and take as settled whatever they see decided by the one they esteem. Nor am I in the habit of approving the practice we are told of among the Pythagoreans, who, when they affirmed something in argument and were asked why it was so, used to answer "He himself said it" — "he himself" being Pythagoras: so much could a preconceived opinion prevail that authority held good even without reason.

But among our forefathers the power of religion was so great that some generals even devoted themselves, with veiled head and in set words, to the immortal gods on behalf of the commonwealth. I could recount many things from the Sibylline prophecies, many from the answers of the soothsayers, by which those things might be confirmed which ought to be doubtful to no one. And indeed both the discipline of our augurs and that of the Etruscan soothsayers was proved by the event itself in the consulship of Publius Scipio and Gaius Figulus. When Tiberius Gracchus, consul for the second time, was holding the election of these men, the first teller, as he reported them, suddenly dropped dead on the spot. Gracchus nonetheless carried through the election; but, perceiving that the matter had caused religious scruple among the people, he referred it to the senate. The senate decreed that it be referred to those to whom such things were usually referred. The soothsayers were brought in and answered that the teller of the election had not been duly qualified. Then Gracchus, as I used to hear from my father, blazed up with anger:

suffer my reason, then, to contend with your reason. You bring all these arguments why the gods exist, and, by arguing, you make a thing, in my opinion by no means doubtful, doubtful; for I have committed to memory not only the number but also the order of your arguments. The first was that, when we had looked up at the sky, we straightway understood that there is some divinity by which these things are ruled. From this came also that: 'Behold this gleaming vault on high, whom all men call upon as Jove':

To those who wonder that I have followed this school in particular, I think a sufficient answer has been given in my four books of Academics. Nor have I taken up the defence of a forsaken and abandoned cause; for opinions do not perish with the death of their authors, though perhaps they want the light an advocate can shed. This method in philosophy, of arguing against all positions and pronouncing openly upon none, set going by Socrates, taken up again by Arcesilas and confirmed by Carneades, has flourished down to our own day; though now I perceive it to be all but orphaned in Greece itself. This I judge to have come about not through any fault of the Academy but through the dullness of men. For if it is a great thing to master single systems, how much greater to master them all — which they must do who have set themselves, for the sake of finding the truth, to speak both against all the philosophers and for them all.

'Is it so indeed — that I, who as consul put the question, and as augur, and with auspices taken, was not duly qualified? But you, Etruscans and barbarians, hold the right of the auspices of the Roman people and can be interpreters of our elections?' And so he then bade them depart. But afterwards he sent from his province a letter to the college, saying that, on reading the books, he had recalled that he had taken his observation-tent improperly in the gardens of Scipio, since, having afterwards crossed the pomerium to hold a meeting of the senate, he had on returning forgotten, when he crossed the same pomerium, to take the auspices; and that therefore the consuls had been elected with a flaw. The augurs referred the matter to the senate; the senate decreed that the consuls should abdicate; they abdicated. What greater examples do we seek? A man most wise, and perhaps the most eminent of all, chose rather to confess his own fault, which might have been concealed, than to let a religious flaw cleave to the commonwealth; and the consuls chose at once to lay down their supreme command rather than hold it for an instant of time against religion.

as though, forsooth, any of us call upon that rather than the Capitoline Jove, or as though it were manifest and agreed among all that those are gods which Velleius and many others would not grant to be even living beings! A weighty argument too seemed to you that the opinion about the immortal gods both belonged to all men and grew daily: is it your pleasure, then, that such great matters be judged by the opinion of fools — and you especially, who say that they are madmen? 'But we see the gods present, as Postumius did at Regillus, Vatinius on the Salarian road' — and I know not what too about the battle of the Locrians at the Sagra. Those, then, whom you called the sons of Tyndareus, that is, men born of man, and whom Homer, who lived not long after their age, says were buried at Lacedaemon — those you suppose to have come to meet Vatinius with white nags and no grooms, and to have announced the victory of the Roman people to Vatinius, a rustic, rather than to Marcus Cato, who was then the chief man? And do you, therefore, believe that mark on the flint which appears to this day at Regillus to be, as it were, the trace of the hoof of Castor's horse?

I do not profess to have attained the capacity for so great and difficult a task; I do claim to have pursued it. Nor yet is it possible that those who philosophise by this method should have nothing to follow. I have indeed spoken of this matter more carefully elsewhere; but because some are too unteachable and slow, they seem to need reminding more than once. We are not men to whom nothing seems true, but men who say that to all truths certain falsehoods are joined, so like them that in them there is no sure mark for judging and assenting. From which it follows also that many things are probable which, though they are not grasped with certainty, yet, because they present an appearance distinct and clear, may guide the life of the wise man.

Great is the authority of the augurs; and the art of the soothsayers — is it not divine? Whoever beholds these things and countless others of the same kind — must he not be compelled to confess that the gods exist? For those of whom there are interpreters must certainly themselves exist; but there are interpreters of the gods; therefore let us confess that the gods exist. But perhaps not all things come to pass that have been foretold. Neither do all the sick recover, and yet medicine is not therefore no art. Signs of things to come are shown by the gods; if any have erred in reading them, it is not the nature of the gods but the conjecture of men that has been at fault. And so among all nations the chief point stands agreed; for it is inborn in all, and as it were graven on the mind, that the gods exist. Of what kind they are is disputed; that they exist no one denies.

Would you not rather believe that which can be proved — that the souls of illustrious men, such as those sons of Tyndareus were, are divine and eternal — than that men once burned could ride and fight in the line of battle? Or, if you say this could have happened, you ought to teach how, and not bring forward old wives' tales."

But now, to free myself from all reproach, I shall set out in full the opinions of the philosophers concerning the nature of the gods. And on this very point all men seem worth summoning to judge which of these opinions is true; then at last shall I think the Academy presumptuous, if either all shall agree, or someone shall be found to have discovered what is true. And so I am moved to cry out, as in the play The Comrades: "In the name of the gods, of all my countrymen, of all the young men, I call, I demand, I beseech, I implore, I lament, and I implore again your aid" — not over some trifling matter, as he there complains that capital crimes are committed in the state: "A courtesan refuses to take money from a lover who loves her" — but that men should be present, should learn, should take note of what is to be thought concerning religion, piety, holiness, ceremonies, good faith and the oath, concerning temples, shrines, and solemn sacrifices, and concerning the very auspices over which I preside (for all these matters bear upon this inquiry into the immortal gods):

Our own Cleanthes, indeed, said that the notions of the gods are formed in the minds of men from four causes. The first he set down was the one I just mentioned, which arose from the forewarning of things to come; the second, that which we have derived from the magnitude of the benefits we receive through the temperateness of the climate, the fruitfulness of the lands, and the abundance of many other advantages;

Then said Lucilius: "Do they seem to you tales? Do you not see the temple dedicated by Aulus Postumius to Castor and Pollux in the forum, do you not see the decree of the senate about Vatinius? As for the Sagra, there is even a common proverb among the Greeks, who say of things they affirm to be more certain than what happened at the Sagra. By these authorities, then, ought you not to be moved?" Then said Cotta: "With rumours you fight against me, Balbus, but I ask reasons of you. [Here several lines are lost.] ... the things that are to be follow;
for assuredly the great disagreement of the most learned men upon the greatest of subjects will compel even those who think they hold something certain to fall into doubt.

the third, that which terrifies our minds with thunderbolts, storms, rainclouds, snow, hail, devastation, pestilence, earthquakes, and often rumblings, showers of stones, and raindrops as it were of blood, then with landslides or sudden gapings of the earth, then with monstrous births of men and beasts contrary to nature, then with heavenly torches seen, then with those stars which the Greeks call comets and our people the long-haired stars (cincinnatae) — which lately, in the war of Octavius, were forerunners of great calamities — then with the doubling of the sun, which, as I heard from my father, happened in the consulship of Tuditanus and Aquilius, the very year in which Publius Africanus, that second sun, was extinguished: by all which men, terrified, suspected that there was some heavenly and divine power;

for no one can escape that which is to be. And often it is not even useful to know what is to be; for it is wretched to be tormented, profiting nothing, and not to have even the last and yet common solace of hope; especially since you yourselves say that all things come to pass by fate, and that what has always been true from all eternity is fate: what avails it, then, or what does it bring toward taking precaution, to know that something is to be, when it is certainly to be? Whence, moreover, comes that divination? Who discovered the cleft of the liver, who marked the song of the crow, who the lots? In which I believe, nor can I despise the augur's staff of Attus Navius which you mentioned; but how these things came to be understood by the philosophers I ought to learn, especially since those diviners lie about very many things.

This I have often observed on other occasions, but most of all when at the house of my friend Gaius Cotta a most careful and searching discussion was held about the immortal gods. For when, during the Latin Holidays, I had come to him at his own request and summons, I found him sitting in his alcove and disputing with Gaius Velleius the senator, to whom at that time the Epicureans assigned the first place among our countrymen. Quintus Lucilius Balbus too was present, who had made such progress in Stoic doctrine as to bear comparison with the most distinguished Greeks in that school. When Cotta saw me he said: "You come most opportunely; for a great debate is just arising between Velleius and me on an important subject, and, knowing your interests, it is not amiss that you should take part."

I shall marvel at the dullness of those who would have a living, immortal, and blessed being be round, on the ground that Plato denies any shape to be fairer than that. But to me a cylinder, or a cube, or a cone, or a pyramid seems more shapely. And what life is assigned to this round god? Surely that he should be whirled about with a speed than which none, not even in thought, can be conceived; and in this I do not see where a steadfast mind and a blessed life can find a resting-place. And whereas in our own body what is felt in the least part is troublesome, why should not the same be held troublesome in a god? For the earth, since it is a part of the world, is also a part of the god; and yet we see vast regions of the earth uninhabited and untilled, part of them scorched by the sun's nearness, part frozen with snow and frost by his distant retreat — so that, if the world is a god, since these are parts of the world, the limbs of the god must be reckoned as partly burning, partly chilled.

This indeed Cleanthes shows by these arguments also — how great a force of heat is in every body: for he denies that there is any food so heavy but that it is digested in a night and a day, and that even in its leavings, which Nature has rejected, there is heat. Then too the veins and arteries do not cease to throb, as it were with a kind of fiery motion, and it has often been observed that when the heart of some animal has been torn out it throbs so swiftly as to imitate the rapidity of fire. Everything, then, that lives, whether animal or sprung from the earth, lives by reason of the heat enclosed in it. From which it ought to be understood that this nature of heat has in itself a vital force pervading the whole world.

And we shall discern this the more easily if the whole of this fiery element which permeates all things is more subtly explained. And why should the soul of man be ignorant of anything, if it were a god? Moreover, how was that god, if he were nothing but soul, either fixed in the world or poured through it? Then Xenophanes, who would have all that exists, with mind added to it and being infinite, to be god, will be censured concerning the mind itself like the rest, and more vehemently concerning the infinite, in which there can be nothing either perceiving or connected. As for Parmenides, he devised something quite fanciful: he makes a thing like a crown — he calls it a stephanê — a continuous ring of glowing light girdling the sky, which he calls god; in which no one could suspect either divine shape or sensation. And there are many other monstrosities of his, since he refers to god War, Discord, Desire, and other things of that kind, which are destroyed by disease or sleep or forgetfulness or age; and the same of the heavenly bodies, which, having been censured in another, may here be passed over.

From which it is concluded that, since all the parts of the world are sustained by heat, the world itself too is preserved by a like and equal nature through so long a span of time; and the more so because we ought to understand that that hot and fiery element is so diffused through all nature that there is in it a force of begetting and a cause of generating, by which both all living things and those whose stems are held in the earth must of necessity be born and grow.

And so that discourse of yours about the harmony and agreement of nature pleased me, which you said breathes in concert, as it were continued by kinship; but that I did not approve, which you said could not have come to pass unless it were held together by one divine spirit. It does, indeed, cohere and abide by the forces of nature, not of the gods, and there is in it that agreement, as it were, which the Greeks call sympatheia; but the more it is of its own accord, the less is it to be thought brought about by a divine reason.

Empedocles, again, who errs in many other matters, falls most shamefully in his opinion of the gods. For he would have the four elements, out of which he holds that all things consist, to be divine; though it is plain that they both come into being and perish and are without all sensation. Nor does Protagoras, who says he has nothing clear to declare about the gods, whether they exist, do not exist, or what they are like, seem to have any conjecture about the nature of the gods. As for Democritus, who at one time reckons images and their revolutions among the gods, at another the nature that pours forth and sends out those images, at another our own thought and understanding — does he not move in the greatest error? And since the same man, on the ground that nothing ever abides in its own state, denies that anything is everlasting, does he not do away with god altogether, so as to leave no notion of him at all? And what of the air, which Diogenes of Apollonia uses as god — what sensation can it have, or what shape of a god?

There is, then, a nature which holds together the whole world and watches over it, and that not without sensation and reason. For every nature which is not solitary nor simple, but joined and connected with another, must have in itself some ruling part, as in man the mind, in the beast something like the mind whence arise the appetites of things; and in trees and the things that grow from the earth the ruling part is thought to reside in the roots. By 'ruling part' I mean that which the Greeks call hegemonikon, than which in each kind nothing can or ought to be more excellent. Thus that too in which is the ruling part of the whole of nature must of necessity be best of all and most worthy of the power and dominion over all things.

But those arguments which Carneades brought forward — how do you dissolve them? If no body is immortal, no body is everlasting; but no body is immortal, not even an indivisible one, nor one that cannot be sundered or torn apart; and since every living being has a nature capable of suffering, there is none of them that escapes the necessity of receiving something from without, that is, as it were, of bearing and suffering; and if every living being is such, none is immortal. So likewise, if every living being can be cut and divided, none of them is indivisible, none eternal; but every living being is fitted for receiving and bearing an external force; therefore every living being must of necessity be mortal and dissoluble and divisible.

It would be long to speak of Plato's inconsistency, who in the Timaeus denies that the father of this world can be named, while in the books of the Laws he holds that we ought not to inquire at all what god is. And as for his wishing god to be without any body (asomaton, as the Greeks say), it cannot be understood how that can be; for he must lack sensation, must lack also prudence, must lack pleasure — all of which we comprehend together with the notion of the gods. The same man, both in the Timaeus and in the Laws, says that the world is a god, and the sky, and the stars, and the earth, and our souls, and those gods whom we have received by the institutions of our forefathers. These statements are both plainly false in themselves and violently at odds with one another.

But we see that in the parts of the world (for there is nothing in the whole world that is not a part of the universe) there is sensation and reason. In that part, then, in which the ruling principle of the world resides, these must necessarily be present, and keener and greater indeed. Wherefore the world must of necessity be wise, and that nature which embraces and holds all things must excel in perfection of reason; and therefore the world is a god, and all the force of the world is held together by the divine nature. And moreover, that heat of the world is purer, more translucent, and far more mobile, and for these reasons fitter to stir the senses than this heat of ours by which the things known to us are upheld and quickened.

For just as, if all wax were changeable, there would be nothing waxen that could not be changed, and likewise nothing silver, nothing of bronze, if the nature of silver and of bronze were changeable — so in like manner, if all things [which exist] of which all are composed are mutable, there can be no body that is not mutable; but those things of which all are composed are mutable, as you hold; every body, therefore, is mutable. But if there were any immortal body, not every body would be mutable; so it follows that every body is mortal. For every body is either water or air or fire or earth, or that which is compounded of these or of some part of them.

Xenophon too, in fewer words, errs in much the same way; for in the sayings which he reported as spoken by Socrates he makes Socrates argue that we ought not to inquire into the shape of god, and the same Socrates call both the sun and the soul a god, and speak now of one god, now of several — which fall into nearly the same mistakes as those we lay to Plato's charge.

It is absurd, then, to say that, while men and beasts are sustained by this heat and thereby move and feel, the world is without sensation, when it is held together by a heat unimpaired, free, and pure, and at the same time most keen and most mobile; especially since that heat which is the world's is moved not stirred by another nor by an external impulse, but of itself and of its own accord; for what can be mightier than the world, to push and move that heat by which the world is held together?

But of these there is none that does not perish; for everything earthy is divisible, and moisture is so soft that it can easily be pressed and crushed; while fire and air are most easily driven off by any blow, and are by nature most yielding and dissipable. And besides, all these perish when they are turned into another nature, which happens when earth turns itself into water, and when from water air arises, from air ether, and when these same pass back again in turn. But if it is so, that those things perish of which every living being consists, no living being is everlasting.

Antisthenes too, in the book entitled Physicus, by saying that there are many gods of popular belief but one god in nature, does away with the power and the nature of the gods. And not much otherwise Speusippus, following his uncle Plato and speaking of a certain force by which all things are governed, and that an animate one, tries to root out from our minds the knowledge of the gods.

For let us hear Plato, as a kind of god of philosophers; who holds that there are two motions, one a thing's own, the other from without, and that what is moved of itself by its own accord is more divine than what is stirred by an alien impulse. This motion he sets only in souls, and thinks the beginning of motion is derived from them. Wherefore, since all motion arises from the heat of the world, and that heat is moved not by an alien impulse but of its own accord, it must be a soul; whence it follows that the world is a living being. And from this too it may be understood that there is intelligence in it, because the world is certainly better than any nature. For as there is no part of our body that is not of less worth than we ourselves are, so the whole world must necessarily be of more worth than any part of the universe. And if this is so, the world must be wise. For if it were not, a man, who is a part of the world, since he partakes of reason, would have to be of more worth than the whole world.

And, to pass over these things, yet no living being can be found which both was never born and will always be. For every living being has sensation; it feels, then, both hot and cold, and sweet and bitter, nor can it by any sense receive the pleasant and not receive the contrary; if, then, it takes the sense of pleasure, it takes also that of pain; but that which receives pain must of necessity receive also destruction; every living being, therefore, must be confessed to be mortal. Besides, if there is anything which feels neither pleasure nor pain, it cannot be a living being;

And Aristotle, in the third book of his Philosophy, throws much into confusion, dissenting from his master Plato; for now he attributes all divinity to mind, now says that the world itself is a god, now sets some other being over the world and assigns it such functions that by a kind of rolling motion it should rule and watch over the movement of the world; then he says that the heat of the heaven is a god, not perceiving that the heaven is a part of the world, which elsewhere he had himself designated as a god. And how can that divine consciousness of the heaven be preserved amid so great a speed? Where, again, are all those gods of his, if we also reckon the heaven a god? And when he likewise would have god be without a body, he strips him of all sensation, and of prudence too. Moreover, how can the world be moved if it is without a body, or how can it, while ever moving itself, be at rest and blessed?

And again, if we wish to proceed from the first and rudimentary natures to the last and most perfect, we must of necessity arrive at the nature of the gods. For first we observe that those things are sustained by Nature which are born from the earth, to which Nature has assigned nothing more than to watch over them by nourishing and increasing them.

but if it is a living being, it must of necessity feel those things, and that which feels them cannot be eternal; and every living being feels; no living being, therefore, is eternal. Besides, there can be no living being in which there is not both a natural appetite and a natural avoidance. But the things that are according to nature are desired, the contrary avoided; and every living being desires some things and flees from some; but that which it flees from is contrary to nature, and that which is contrary to nature has the power of destroying. Every living being, therefore, must of necessity perish.

Nor indeed is his fellow-pupil Xenocrates wiser in this kind; in whose books on the nature of the gods no divine form is described. For he says there are eight gods: five, those named among the wandering stars; one, to be reckoned a single god composed of all the fixed stars set in the sky, as out of scattered limbs; to which he joins the sun as a seventh and the moon as an eighth — though in what sense these can be blessed cannot be understood. From the same school of Plato, Heraclides of Pontus crammed his books with childish fables, and yet at one time thinks the world, at another the divine mind, to be god; he also gives divinity to the wandering stars, deprives god of sensation, will have his shape be changeable, and in the same book again reckons earth and sky among the gods.

But to the beasts she gave sensation and motion, and, along with a kind of appetite, an approach to wholesome things and a withdrawal from harmful. To man she added something more — reason, by which the appetites of the soul should be governed, now slackened, now restrained. There is yet a fourth and highest grade, of those who are born by nature good and wise, in whom from the beginning is implanted a right and steadfast reason, which must be reckoned above man and assigned to god, that is, to the world, in which that perfect and absolute reason must of necessity reside.

Innumerable are the things from which it can be brought about and concluded that there is nothing which has sensation but it perishes; for those very things which are felt — as cold, as heat, as pleasure, as pain, and the rest — when they are amplified, destroy; and no living being is without sensation; no living being, therefore, is eternal. For either the nature of a living being is simple — so that it is either earthy or fiery or airy or moist, which, of what kind it would be, cannot even be understood — or compounded of several natures, of which each has its own place to which it is borne by the force of nature, one to the lowest, another to the highest, another to the middle. These can cohere for a certain time, but always in no way can they; for each must of necessity be snatched by nature to its own place. No living being, therefore, is everlasting.

Nor is the inconsistency of Theophrastus to be borne; for now he gives the divine sovereignty to mind, now to the sky, now to the signs and heavenly bodies. Nor is his pupil Strato — he who is called the natural philosopher — to be listened to, who holds that all divine power resides in nature, which has the causes of generating, increasing, and diminishing, but is without all sensation and shape.

For it cannot be said that in any ordering of things there is not something final and perfect. For as in the vine, as in the herd, unless some force opposes, we see Nature by a certain path of her own arrive at the utmost; and as painting and building and the other arts have a certain effecting of a finished work, so in all nature, and much more so, something must of necessity be brought to completion and perfection. And indeed in the other natures many external things may hinder them from being perfected, but nothing can impede universal Nature, for the reason that she herself contains and holds together all natures. Wherefore there must be that fourth and highest grade, to which no force can come near.

But your school, Balbus, is wont to refer all things to a fiery force, following, I believe, Heraclitus, whom not all interpret in one way; and since he meant something which he did not wish to be understood, let us pass him by. But you say thus, that all force is fire, and so that living beings perish when their heat has failed, and that in all the nature of things that lives, that flourishes, which is warm. But I do not understand how, the heat being quenched, bodies perish, but do not perish when moisture or breath is lost — especially since they perish even by too much heat.

Zeno, however — to come now, Balbus, to your school — holds that the natural law is divine, and that it has the power of commanding what is right and forbidding the contrary. But how he makes this law a living being we cannot understand; and a god we certainly mean to be a living being. The same man elsewhere calls the ether a god — if a god can be conceived that has no sensation, that never meets us in our prayers, our wishes, or our vows. In other books he holds that a certain reason pervading the whole nature of things is endowed with divine power. He gives this same attribute to the stars, then to the years, the months, and the changes of the seasons. And when he interprets Hesiod's Theogony — that is, the origin of the gods — he abolishes altogether the customary and received notions of the gods; for he reckons neither Jupiter, nor Juno, nor Vesta, nor anyone so named among the gods, but teaches that these names have been assigned, by a kind of symbolism, to lifeless and dumb things.

And this is the grade in which is placed the nature of all things; which, since it is such that it both presides over all and nothing can hinder it, must of necessity be intelligent, and indeed wise too. For what is more ignorant than to say that that nature which has embraced all things is not best, or, being best, is not first a living being, then endowed with reason and counsel, and finally wise? For how can it otherwise be best? For if it were like the plants or even like the beasts, it would have to be thought not best but rather worst. And again, if it partook of reason yet were not wise from the beginning, the condition of the world would be worse rather than human. For a man can become wise, but the world, if through the eternal span of past time it was unwise, will surely never attain wisdom; thus it would be worse than man. And since this is absurd, the world must be held both wise from the beginning and a god.

Wherefore that point indeed is common, about the hot; but yet let us see the issue. You mean, I suppose, that there is no living being from without in nature and the world save fire: why so, rather than save breath, of which too the soul of living beings consists, from which a thing is called animal? But how do you assume, as if it were granted, that the soul is nothing but fire? For it seems more probable that the soul is some such thing as is tempered of fire and breath. 'But if fire is of itself a living being, with no other nature mingling itself, since it, when it is in our bodies, makes us feel, it cannot itself be without sensation.' Again the same things may be said: for whatever has sensation must of necessity feel both pleasure and pain, and that to which pain comes, to the same comes also destruction. So it comes about that you cannot make even fire eternal.

The opinion of his pupil Aristo is in no less great an error, who holds that the shape of god cannot be understood, denies that there is sensation in the gods, and is altogether in doubt whether god is a living being or not. Cleanthes, again, who studied under Zeno together with the one I just named, at one time says the world itself is a god, at another gives this name to the mind and soul of the whole of nature, at another judges that the uttermost and highest heat, poured round about on every side, embracing and enclosing all things on the outside, which is called ether, is most surely a god; and, as if raving, in the books he wrote against Pleasure, he now invents a kind of form and aspect of the gods, now assigns all divinity to the stars, now holds that nothing is more divine than reason. And so it comes about that that god whom we know by the mind and would set, as it were, in the impression of the soul as in a footprint, nowhere appears at all. But Persaeus, also a pupil of the same Zeno, held that those have been counted gods by whom some great benefit to the comforts of life had been discovered, and that useful and wholesome things themselves were called by the names of gods — so that he did not even say that those things were the discoveries of gods, but that they were themselves divine;

For there is nothing else besides the world to which nothing is lacking, and which is on every side fitted, perfect, and complete in all its numbers and parts. For Chrysippus aptly says that, as the case is for the sake of the shield and the sheath for the sake of the sword, so, except the world, all other things were generated for the sake of others — as the crops and fruits which the earth brings forth for the sake of living creatures, and living creatures for the sake of men, as the horse for carrying, the ox for ploughing, the dog for hunting and guarding; but man himself was born to contemplate and imitate the world — by no means perfect, but a kind of small particle of the perfect.

For what — do not you Stoics hold that all fire needs nourishment and cannot endure in any way unless it is fed, but that the sun, moon, and the other heavenly bodies are fed by waters, some by fresh, some by sea-water? And Cleanthes brings forward this as the reason why the sun turns back and does not advance farther than the solstitial circle, and likewise the wintry, lest it should depart too far from its food. What this whole matter is like, presently; but for now let that be concluded: that what can perish is not by nature eternal; but fire is going to perish unless it is fed; fire, therefore, is not by nature everlasting.

than which what could be more absurd, either to invest base and unsightly things with the honour of gods, or to set among the gods men already swept away by death, whose every worship would be a matter of mourning?

But the world, since it has embraced all things, and there is nothing which is not contained in it, is perfect on every side; how, then, can that be lacking to it which is best? But nothing is better than mind and reason; therefore these cannot be lacking to the world. Well, then, does the same Chrysippus, adding comparisons, teach that all things are better in the perfect and the mature — as in the horse than in the colt, in the dog than in the puppy, in the man than in the boy; likewise that what is best in the whole world must reside in something perfect and complete;

But what kind of god can we understand who is endowed with no virtue? For what — shall we assign prudence to god, which consists of the knowledge of things good and bad, and of things neither good nor bad? For one to whom there is no evil, nor can be, what need has he of choosing between good and bad, and what of reason, what of intelligence — which we use for this end, that from things plain we may attain things obscure? But to god nothing can be obscure. For justice, which distributes to each his own, what has it to do with the gods? For the fellowship and community of men, as you say, begot justice. But temperance consists in the foregoing of bodily pleasures: if there is a place for this in heaven, there is a place also for pleasures. For how can god be understood to be brave — in pain, or in toil, or in danger?

And now Chrysippus, who is held to be the shrewdest interpreter of the Stoics' dreams, gathers a great throng of unknown gods, and so unknown that we cannot even by conjecture form a picture of them, though our mind seems able to paint anything it pleases by thought. For he says that the divine power resides in reason and in the soul and mind of universal nature; he says the world itself is a god, and the universal diffusion of its soul; then the ruling part of that very soul, which dwells in mind and reason; then the common nature of things, universal and containing all things; then fate and the necessity of things to come; besides, fire, and that ether of which I spoke before; then the things that flow and stream by nature, such as water, earth, and air; the sun, moon, and stars, and the totality of things by which all are contained; and even those men who have attained immortality.

but there is nothing more perfect than the world, nothing better than virtue; therefore virtue is proper to the world. Nor indeed is the nature of man perfect, and yet virtue is brought about in man; how much more easily, then, in the world! There is, therefore, virtue in it. The world, then, is wise, and for that reason a god. And, this divinity of the world being perceived, the same divinity must be assigned to the heavenly bodies, which are generated from the most mobile and purest part of the ether, and have besides no other nature mingled in, and are wholly hot and translucent, so that they too may most rightly be said both to be living and to feel and understand.

Of which none touches god. Neither, then, can we understand god to be one using reason nor endowed with any virtue. Nor indeed can I despise the ignorance of the common folk and the unlearned, when I consider those things which are said by the Stoics. For those things are of the ignorant: the Syrians worship a fish; the Egyptians have consecrated almost every kind of beast; and now in Greece they have many gods made out of men — Alabandus at Alabanda, at Tenedos Tenes; Leucothea, who was Ino, and her son Palaemon, all Greece worships — as well as Hercules, Aesculapius, the sons of Tyndareus, our own Romulus, and very many others, whom they think received into heaven as it were new and enrolled citizens.

The same man argues that the ether is what men call Jupiter; that the air which streams through the seas is Neptune; that the earth is what is called Ceres; and in like fashion he traces out the names of the rest of the gods. The same man also says that Jupiter is the force of perpetual and eternal law, which is, as it were, the guide of life and the mistress of duties; and he calls the same the fated necessity, the everlasting truth of things to come — none of which is of such a kind that any divine power can be seen to reside in it.

And that they are wholly fiery, Cleanthes thinks is confirmed by the testimony of two senses, touch and sight. For the heat and brightness of the sun is more brilliant than that of any fire, since it shines so far and wide through the boundless world; and its touch is such that it not only warms but often even burns — neither of which it would do unless it were fiery. 'Therefore,' he says, 'since the sun is fiery and is fed by the moisture of the Ocean' (for no fire can endure without some nourishment), 'it must of necessity be either like that fire which we employ for use and for living, or like that which is contained in the bodies of living creatures.

These things, then, the unlearned hold; what of you philosophers, who hold better things? I pass over those — for they are excellent: let the world itself, by all means, be a god. This, I believe, is that 'gleaming vault on high, whom all men call upon as Jove.' Why, then, do we add more gods? And how great is their multitude! To me, indeed, they seem very many; for you reckon the single stars to be gods, and call them either by the name of beasts — as the Goat, the Scorpion, the Bull, the Lion — or of lifeless things, as Argo, the Altar, the Crown.

And this indeed in his first book on the nature of the gods; while in the second he sets out to accommodate the fables of Orpheus, Musaeus, Hesiod, and Homer to what he himself had said in the first book about the immortal gods, so that even the most ancient poets, who never so much as suspected these things, may seem to have been Stoics. Following him, Diogenes of Babylon, in the book entitled On Minerva, by referring the birth of Jupiter and the origin of the virgin goddess to natural science, severs them from the fable.

But this fire of ours, which the use of life requires, is the destroyer and consumer of all things, and wherever it has invaded, it disorders and scatters everything; whereas that bodily fire, vital and wholesome, preserves all things, nourishes, increases, sustains, and gives sensation.' He denies, then, that there is any doubt to which of these fires the sun is like, since it too makes all things flourish and each kind grow to ripeness. Wherefore, since the fire of the sun is like those fires which are in the bodies of living creatures, the sun too must be a living being, and likewise the rest of the stars which arise in that heavenly heat which is called ether or sky.

But, granting these, how can the rest not only be granted but even at all understood? When we call the crops Ceres and wine Liber, we use indeed a customary manner of speech; but do you think anyone so mad as to believe that the thing he feeds on is a god? As for those whom you say came from men to be gods, you shall render account in what way that could have come to pass, or why it ceased to come to pass, and I shall gladly learn; for as the matter now stands, I do not see how he upon whom 'on Mount Oeta the torches were borne,' as Accius says, came from that burning 'to the eternal house of his father'; whom yet Homer makes to be met among the dead by Ulysses, like the rest who had departed life.

I have now set forth, in effect, not the judgements of philosophers but the dreams of madmen. For these are scarcely more absurd than the things which, poured out in the words of the poets, have done harm by their very charm — poets who have brought in gods inflamed with anger and raging with lust, and have made us behold their wars, battles, combats, and wounds; their hatreds besides, their dissensions and discords, their births and deaths, their complaints and lamentations, their lusts let loose in every kind of intemperance, their adulteries and bonds, their unions with the human race, and mortals begotten of immortals.

Since, then, the birth of some living creatures is in the earth, of some in water, of some in air, it seems absurd to Aristotle to think that no living thing is generated in that part which is best fitted for generating living creatures. But the heavenly bodies hold the ethereal region; and since this is most subtle and ever in motion and full of vigour, the living thing that is generated in it must of necessity be of the keenest sensation and the swiftest mobility. Wherefore, since the stars are generated in the ether, it is consistent that there should be sensation and intelligence in them; from which it follows that the stars are to be reckoned in the number of the gods. And indeed it may be observed that the minds of those who dwell in lands where the air is pure and thin are keener and apter for understanding than those of men who breathe a thick and clogged air.

And yet which Hercules above all we should worship I should much like to know; for several are handed down to us by those who search out the inner and hidden lore: the most ancient born of Jove — but likewise of the most ancient Jove, for we find several Joves too in the ancient writings of the Greeks: of that one, then, and of Lysitho, is that Hercules whom we have heard to have striven with Apollo for the tripod. A second is handed down, an Egyptian born of the Nile, who is said to have written the Phrygian letters. The third is of the Idaean Dactyls, to whom they bring funeral offerings. The fourth is of Jove and of Asteria, sister of Latona, who is worshipped most at Tyre, whose daughter they say Carthage was. The fifth is in India, who is called Belus. The sixth is this one, born of Alcmena, whom Jupiter begot — but the third Jupiter, since, as I shall presently show, we have received several Joves too.

With the error of the poets we may join the portents of the Magi and the madness of the Egyptians in the same kind, and then also the opinions of the common folk, which, through ignorance of the truth, dwell in the greatest inconstancy. Whoever considers how thoughtlessly and rashly these things are said ought to revere Epicurus and to reckon him among the very persons of whom this inquiry treats. For he alone saw, first, that the gods exist, because Nature herself has imprinted a notion of them in the minds of all. For what nation or what kind of men is there that does not have, without instruction, a certain anticipation of the gods — what Epicurus calls prolepsis, that is, a kind of outline of the thing grasped beforehand by the mind, without which nothing can be understood, inquired into, or argued about? The force and usefulness of this principle we have learned from that heavenly volume of Epicurus On the Standard and Judgement.

Nay, they think that even the food one uses makes some difference to the keenness of the mind. It is probable, then, that there is a surpassing intelligence in the heavenly bodies, which both dwell in the ethereal part of the world and are fed by the moistures of sea and earth, refined by their long passage. But the sensation and intelligence of the stars is most clearly declared by their order and constancy (for there is nothing that can be moved by measure and number without counsel), in which there is nothing rash, nothing variable, nothing fortuitous. And the order of the heavenly bodies and their constancy through all eternity signify neither nature (for that is full of reason) nor fortune, which, being friendly to variety, rejects constancy. It follows, then, that they move of their own accord, by their own sensation and divinity.

For, since the discourse has led me to this place, I will show that I have learned better things about worshipping the immortal gods, by the pontifical law and the custom of our forefathers, from these little ladles which Numa left us, of which Laelius speaks in that golden little oration, than from the reasonings of the Stoics. For if I follow you, tell me what I should answer to one who asks me thus: 'If the gods exist [...], are the Nymphs also goddesses? If the Nymphs, the Pans too and the Satyrs; but these are not; therefore not even the Nymphs are goddesses. Yet their temples are publicly vowed and dedicated. Neither, then, are the rest gods whose temples are dedicated. Come further: you reckon Jove and Neptune a god; therefore Orcus too, their brother, is a god, and those who are said to flow in the underworld, Acheron, Cocytus, Pyriphlegethon; then Charon, then Cerberus must be thought gods.

You see, then, that the foundation of this inquiry has been splendidly laid. For since the belief has been established by no convention, custom, or law, and there remains a firm agreement of all men to a man, it must be understood that the gods exist, because we have implanted, or rather inborn, notions of them; and that on which the nature of all agrees must of necessity be true. The existence of the gods, therefore, must be confessed. And since this is generally agreed not only among philosophers but among the unlearned too, we confess that this too is agreed: that we have this anticipation, as I said before, or prenotion of the gods — for to new things new names must be given, as Epicurus himself called it prolepsis,

Nor indeed is Aristotle not to be praised for this, that he held that all things which move are moved either by nature, or by force, or by will; that the sun and moon and all the stars move; that things moved by nature are borne either downward by weight or upward by lightness — neither of which befalls the stars, because their motion is borne round in a circle; nor can it be said that it comes about by some greater force that the stars move contrary to nature (for what force can be greater?); it remains, then, that the motion of the stars is voluntary. And he who sees this would act not only ignorantly but impiously if he should deny that the gods exist. Nor does it much matter whether he denies it or strips them of all care and action; for to me one who does nothing seems not to exist at all. That the gods, then, exist is so manifest that I should hardly count him of sound mind who denies it.

But that indeed must be rejected; not even Orcus, then, is a god; what, then, do you say of the brothers?' These things Carneades said, not to do away with the gods (for what is less becoming a philosopher?), but to prove that the Stoics explain nothing about the gods; and so he pressed on: 'For what,' he said, 'if these brothers are in the number of the gods, can it be denied of their father Saturn, whom the common folk worship most of all toward the west? But if he is a god, his father Caelus too must be confessed to be a god. And if it is so, the parents of Caelus too must be held gods, Aether and Day, and their brothers and sisters, who by the ancient genealogists are named thus: Love, Guile, Fear, Toil, Envy, Fate, Old Age, Death, Darkness, Misery, Lamentation, Favour, Fraud, Stubbornness, the Fates, the Hesperides, the Dreams; all of whom they say were born of Erebus and Night. Either, then, these monstrosities must be approved, or those first ones done away with.'

a thing which no one before had named by that word — this anticipation, then, we have, namely that we think the gods blessed and immortal. For the same Nature that gave us the outline of the gods themselves has graven it on our minds that we should hold them eternal and blessed. And if this is so, then that maxim of Epicurus has been truly set forth: that what is blessed and eternal neither has any trouble itself nor causes any to another, and is therefore held neither by anger nor by favour, since all such things belong to weakness. If we were seeking nothing else than to worship the gods piously and to be freed from superstition, enough would have been said; for the surpassing nature of the gods would be worshipped by the piety of men, being both eternal and most blessed (for whatever excels has a just claim to reverence), and all fear of the violence and anger of the gods would have been driven off; for it is understood that both anger and favour are removed from a blessed and immortal nature, and that, these removed, no terrors hang over us from on high. But to confirm this opinion, the mind seeks both the form and the life of the gods, and the working and activity of their mind.

It remains to consider of what kind their nature is; in which nothing is harder than to draw the mind's keen sight away from the habit of the eyes. This difficulty has led both the ignorant common folk, and philosophers like the ignorant, to be unable to conceive anything of the immortal gods save in the established shapes of men; the shallowness of which opinion, refuted by Cotta, needs no discourse of mine. But since by a sure conception of the mind we forefeel that god is such — first, that he is a living being, and next, that in all nature there is nothing more excellent than he — to this our forefeeling and conception I see nothing I can better fit than to judge, first, this very world, than which nothing more excellent can be, to be a living being and a god.

Will you say that Apollo, Vulcan, Mercury, and the rest are gods, but doubt about Hercules, Aesculapius, Liber, Castor, and Pollux? But these indeed are worshipped equally with those, and among some peoples even much more. These, then, must be held gods, though born of mortal mothers. What of Aristaeus, who is said to be the discoverer of the olive, the son of Apollo; Theseus, who was the son of Neptune; and the rest whose fathers are gods — will they not be in the number of the gods? What of those whose mothers are goddesses? Even more so, I think; for as in the civil law he who is born of a free mother is free, so by the law of nature he who is of a divine mother must of necessity be a god. And so the islanders of Astypalaea most devoutly worship Achilles; but if he is a god, then Orpheus and Rhesus too are gods, born of a Muse for their mother — unless, perhaps, marriages with sea-deities are set above those with earthly ones. If these are not gods, because they are nowhere worshipped, how are those?

Which, if Epicurus had learned how many twice two is, he certainly would not say; but while he judges with his palate what is best, he never looked up to the 'palate of the heaven,' as Ennius says. And first the sun, which holds the chief place among the stars, moves so that, when it has filled the lands with its broad light, it shadows the same now from these parts now from those; for the shadow of the earth itself, falling across the sun, makes the night. And the evenness of the nightly spaces is the same as that of the daily. And the moderate approaches and retreats of the same sun temper the measure of cold and heat. For the circuits of three hundred and sixty-five revolutions of the sun's orbit, with about a fourth part of a day added, complete the yearly revolution; and the sun, bending its course now to the north, now to the south, makes summers and winters and those two seasons of which one is joined to declining winter, the other to summer: so that from the changes of the four seasons are derived the beginnings and causes of all things that are born on land and sea.

This god we may rightly call blessed; but yours we may call most toilsome. But what does your Epicurus say (for I would rather argue with him than with you) that is worthy not merely of philosophy but of common prudence? 'Without Ceres and Liber, Venus grows cold' — and at another time the thing itself, in which there is some greater force, is so named that the very force is called a god, as Faith, as Mind, which we see dedicated on the Capitol, the one quite lately by Marcus Aemilius Scaurus, while Faith had been consecrated earlier by Aulus Atilius Calatinus. You see the temple of Virtue, you see that of Honour, renewed by Marcus Marcellus, which many years before had been dedicated by Quintus Maximus in the Ligurian war. What of Plenty, what of Safety, of Concord, of Liberty, of Victory? Since the force of all these was so great that it could not be governed without a god, the thing itself obtained the name of a god. For we see that Mind, Faith, Hope, Virtue, Honour, Victory, Safety, Concord, and the rest of this kind have the force of things, not of gods. For either they are in us ourselves — as mind, as hope, as faith, as virtue, as concord — or they are to be wished for by us, as honour, as safety, as victory; of which things I see the usefulness, I see also the consecrated images; but why there should be the force of a god in them I shall understand when I have learned it. In which kind fortune above all is to be reckoned, whom no one will sever from inconstancy and rashness — things which surely are not worthy of a god.

But see how generously I deal with you: what you have in common with the other philosophers I will not touch, as this very point; for it is agreed by almost all, and by me first of all, that the gods exist. And so I do not contend on that head; yet the argument you bring forward I do not think firm enough. You said that the fact that it seems so to men of all nations and kinds is a sufficiently great proof why we should confess the gods to exist. But this is both weak in itself and also false. For, first, whence are the opinions of the nations known to you? For my part I think there are many peoples so brutalised by savagery that among them there is no notion of gods at all.

By the greatness of their usefulness, then, were those gods established who generated the several advantages; and indeed by those names which were just now mentioned the force that is in each god is declared. The life and common custom of men, moreover, have taken it up to raise to heaven, by fame and goodwill, men eminent in benefits. Hence Hercules, hence Castor and Pollux, hence Aesculapius, hence Liber too (I mean the Liber born of Semele, not him whom our forefathers solemnly and reverently consecrated as Liber with Ceres and Libera, the nature of which may be understood from the mysteries; but because we call our children liberi, born of us, Liber and Libera were named as born of Ceres, a thing they preserve in the case of Libera but not so in that of Liber) — hence too Romulus, whom some think to be the same as Quirinus. Since the souls of these remained and enjoyed eternity, they were rightly held to be gods, being both most excellent and eternal.

And now, what delights you in that unfolding of fables and untying of names? That Caelus was mutilated by his son, that Saturn likewise was bound by his son — these things and others of the same kind you so defend that those who invented them seem not only not mad but even to have been wise. But in untying names you labour at what is pitiable: 'Saturn, because he sates himself with years; Mavors, because he turns great things; Minerva, because she lessens, or because she threatens; Venus, because she comes to all things; Ceres, from bearing.'
