How dangerous a practice! For in many names you will stick fast: what will you make of Veiovis, what of Vulcan? Although, since you think Neptune named from swimming, there will be no name which you cannot explain, by one letter, whence it is drawn; in which indeed you seemed to me to swim more than Neptune himself.

What of Diagoras, who was called the Atheist, and afterwards Theodorus — did they not openly do away with the nature of the gods? Nay, Protagoras of Abdera, of whom you made mention just now, perhaps the greatest sophist of those times, having set down at the beginning of his book "Of the gods I am not able to say either that they are or that they are not," was by decree of the Athenians banished from city and country, and his books burned in the assembly; from which I for my part suppose that many were made the slower to profess this opinion, since not even doubt could escape punishment. And what shall we say of the sacrilegious, the impious, the perjured? If Lucius Tubulus, or Lupus, or Carbo, or the son of Neptune, as Lucilius says, had ever thought there were gods, would they have been so perjured or so foul?

From another reasoning too, and that a physical one, a great multitude of gods has flowed, who, clad in human shape, have furnished fables to the poets and stuffed the life of men with every superstition. And this topic, handled by Zeno, was afterwards expounded at greater length by Cleanthes and Chrysippus. For this old opinion filled Greece, that Caelus was mutilated by his son Saturn, and Saturn himself bound by his son Jove:

A great and least necessary toil did Zeno first, then Cleanthes, then Chrysippus take upon themselves — to render the reason of invented fables, to explain the causes why each thing was so named. And in doing this you assuredly confess that the matter stands far otherwise than is the opinion of men; for those who are called gods are the natures of things, not the figures of gods. So great was the error that even to pernicious things not only the name of gods was given but even rites were established. For we see a shrine of Fever on the Palatine, and of Orbona near the temple of the Lares, and an altar of Evil Fortune consecrated on the Esquiline.

Your argument, then, is not so well established for confirming what you wish as it seems. But since this argument is common to other philosophers also, I will pass it over for now; I prefer to come to what is properly yours.

a not inelegant physical reasoning is shut up in these impious fables. For they meant that the highest and ethereal — that is, the fiery — nature of the heaven, which of itself generated all things, was free from that part of the body which would need conjunction with another for procreating. And they meant Saturn to be that which contains the course and revolution of spaces and times. Which god has in Greek that very name: for he is called Kronos, who is the same as chronos, that is, a space of time. But Saturn was so named because he is sated (saturaretur) with years; for he is feigned to have been wont to devour his own offspring, because time consumes the spaces of the seasons and is insatiably filled with the years that are past. And he was bound by Jove, lest he should have immoderate courses, and that Jove might bind him with the chains of the stars. But Jupiter himself — that is, the helping father (iuvans pater), whom, with the cases turned, we call Jove (Iovem) from helping (a iuvando), is by the poets called 'father of gods and men,' and by our forefathers 'best and greatest,' and indeed 'best,' that is, most beneficent, before 'greatest,' because it is greater and surely more pleasing to benefit all than to have great wealth —

Let all such error, then, be driven from philosophy, so that, when we discuss the immortal gods, we may say things worthy of the immortal gods. About whom I have indeed what I myself think, but I have not what to grant you. You say that Neptune is a soul with intelligence pervading the sea, the same of Ceres; but that intelligence either of sea or of earth I cannot only not grasp with my mind but cannot even touch with surmise. And so I must seek elsewhere, that I may learn both that the gods exist and of what kind the gods are, such as you would have them be [...].

I grant that the gods exist; teach me, then, whence they are, where they are, what they are like in body, in soul, in life; for these things I desire to know. You make use of the realm and licence of atoms for everything; out of them you fashion and produce whatever, as the saying goes, falls to the ground. First of all, these atoms do not exist. For there is nothing void of body, and every place is besieged by bodies; so there can be no void, and nothing can be indivisible.

this Jupiter, then, Ennius, as I said above, names, saying thus: 'Behold this gleaming vault on high, whom all men call upon as Jove,' more plainly than in another place the same poet: 'I will curse this — whatsoever it is that shines — with all that is in me.' Him too our augurs mean when they say 'Jove flashing, thundering'; for they say 'the sky flashing and thundering.' And Euripides, as in many places admirably, so here briefly: 'You see the boundless ether spread on high, that with its tender embrace clasps the earth round about: hold this the highest of the gods, call this Jove.'

[...] let us see the things that follow: first, whether the world is ruled by the prudence of the gods; next, whether the gods take thought for human affairs. For these two remain to me out of your partition; of which, if it seems good to you, I think we must discuss more carefully." "To me indeed," said Velleius, "it seems very good; for I both expect greater things and vehemently assent to what has been said." Then said Balbus: "I do not wish to interrupt you, Cotta, but we will take another time; I will assuredly bring it about that you confess. But [here several lines are lost] ... In the first place, then, it is not probable that that matter of things, whence all things arose, was made by divine providence, but that it both has and has had its own force and nature. As, then, a builder, when he is about to build something, does not himself make the material but uses that which is ready, and likewise the modeller his wax, so to that divine providence the material ought to have been ready at hand, not such as it should itself make but such as it should have prepared. But if the matter was not made by a god, neither was the earth, nor the water, nor the air, nor the fire made by a god. [Here the text is corrupt; a fragment of a tragic passage follows, in which a character, debating with cunning, plots a deadly course:] ... men surpass all the beasts ... in no wise will it go that way; great is the strife within. For why should I beseech him with such fair-spoken pleading, if not for a purpose? Does she not seem to reason but ill, and to contrive against herself a wicked ruin?

I now pour forth these oracles of the natural philosophers, whether true or false I know not, but more like the truth than yours. For those scandalous notions of Democritus, or even before him of Leucippus, that there are certain particles, some smooth, some rough, some round, some angular and hooked, some curved and as it were bent inward, and that of these were made the sky and the earth, with no nature compelling but by a kind of chance concourse — this opinion, Gaius Velleius, you have prolonged down to our own age, and one would sooner unseat you from every standing in life than from this authority; for you judged that you must be an Epicurean before you came to know these doctrines. Thus it was necessary either to take these scandals into your mind or to give up the name of the philosophy you had embraced.

The air, moreover, as the Stoics argue, lying between sea and sky, is consecrated under the name of Juno, who is the sister and wife of Jove, because it both has a likeness to the ether and is most closely joined with it. And they made it feminine and assigned it to Juno, because nothing is softer than it. But Juno, I believe, was named from helping (a iuvando). Water remained and earth, that there might be three realms divided according to the fables. To Neptune, then, the brother of Jove, as we will have it, was given the second, the whole realm of the sea; and his name was drawn, as Portunus from porta (a gate), so Neptune from swimming (a nando), the first letters being a little changed. But all the earthly force and nature was dedicated to Father Dis, who is the rich one — as among the Greeks Plouton — because all things both fall back into the earth and arise from the earth. To whom Proserpina (which is a Greek name, for she is the one who is called in Greek Persephone) — whom they will have to be the seed of the crops, and feign to be hidden and sought by her mother.

And how with cunning reasoning: 'Whoever wishes what he wishes, the matter so gives itself as he shall give his pains' — who is the sower of all evils. He, with crooked mind, has this day delivered to me the bars by which I shall unbar all my wrath and bring ruin upon him: griefs to myself, mourning to him; destruction to him, exile to me. This reasoning, forsooth, which you say was given to man alone by the divine bounty, the beasts have not; do you see, then, with how great a gift of the gods we have been endowed?

For what would you take to cease being an Epicurean? "Nothing indeed," you say, "to make me forsake the plan of the blessed life and the truth." Is that, then, the truth? For about the blessed life I make no objection — that life which you hold not to exist even in a god unless he languishes in sheer idleness. But where is the truth? In countless worlds, I suppose, some coming to birth and some falling away at every least point of time? Or in indivisible particles fashioning so splendid a work with no Nature to guide, no reason to shape? But, forgetting that generosity which I began to show you a little while ago, I am taking in more than I need. I will grant, then, that all things consist of indivisible particles; what is that to the matter?

And her mother is Ceres, from the bearing of crops (a gerendis frugibus), as if geres, the first letter being likewise changed, as among the Greeks; for by them too she was named Demeter, as if ge meter (mother earth). And he who turns great things (qui magna verteret) is Mavors, while Minerva is she who either lessens (minueret) or threatens (minaretur). And since in all things the first and the last have the greatest force, they would have Janus be foremost in sacrificing, whose name is drawn from going (ab eundo), whence the open passages are called iani and the doors at the thresholds of profane houses ianuae. The name of Vesta is from the Greeks (for she is the one who is called by them Hestia); but her force pertains to altars and hearths, and so in this goddess, who is the keeper of the inmost things, every prayer and every sacrifice ends.

And the same Medea, fleeing her father and her fatherland, when her father draws near and is already all but ready to seize her, meanwhile slays the boy and divides his limbs joint by joint, and scatters his body here and there over the fields; to this end, that, while the parent gathered up the scattered limbs of his son, she herself might meanwhile escape, that mourning might delay him from following, and that she might procure safety for herself by a kinsman's murder. To her, as wickedness, so reason too was not lacking.

For it is the nature of the gods that is in question. Let them, by all means, be made of atoms; then they are not eternal. For if of atoms, then they came into being at some time; if they came into being, there were no gods before they were born; and if the gods have had a beginning, they must of necessity have an end, as you yourself argued a little while ago about Plato's world. Where, then, is that "blessed and eternal" of yours, by which two words you signify a god? And when you try to make this good, you creep into thorn-brakes. For so you said: that there is in god not body but as it were body, not blood but as it were blood.

Nor far from this force are the Penates, whose name is drawn either from penus (for everything on which men feed is penus) or from their dwelling deep within (penitus); whence too they are called by the poets penetrales. Now the name of Apollo is Greek; whom they will have to be the sun, and they think Diana and the moon to be the same; the sun being so called either because it is the only one (solus) of all the stars of such size, or because, when it has risen, all else being darkened, it alone appears; and the moon (luna) being named from shining (a lucendo); for she is the same as Lucina, and so, as among the Greeks they call upon Diana, and her as Lucifera, so among our people they call upon Juno Lucina in childbirth. The same Diana is called Omnivaga (the all-wandering), not from hunting (a venando) but because she is reckoned among the seven, as it were, wandering bodies;

And he who prepared the deadly banquet for his brother — does he not turn his reasoning this way and that in thought? 'A greater mass is mine, a greater evil must be mingled, by which I may crush and press down his bitter heart.' Nor yet must that one himself be passed over, who was not content to have lured the other's wife into adultery; of whom Atreus speaks rightly and most truly: 'What I judge to be, in the highest matter, the highest peril — that the wives of kings be defiled, the stock contaminated, the race confounded.' But that very thing, how cunningly, in one who sought a kingdom by adultery! 'I add,' he says, 'to this, that as a portent the father of the heavenly ones sent me a prodigy, the prop of my reign, a lamb among the flock, bright with golden fleece, which Thyestes once dared to steal from the palace, wherein he took my wife to aid him in the deed.' Does he not seem to have used, with the height of wickedness, no small height of reason?

This you very often do — that, when you say something not likely and wish to escape censure, you bring in something that cannot possibly even come to be, so that it would have been better to grant the very point at issue than to resist so shamelessly. Thus Epicurus, when he saw that, if the atoms were borne downward by their own weight, nothing would be in our power, since their motion would be fixed and necessary, found a way to escape necessity — a thing which had plainly escaped Democritus: he says that the atom, while it is carried straight downward by its weight and gravity, swerves a very little.

Diana so called because by night she makes, as it were, a day (quasi diem). And she is invoked at births, because these come to maturity sometimes in seven, but for the most part in nine, courses of the moon, which, because they complete measured spaces (mensa spatia), are called months (menses); and, neatly, as Timaeus does many things, who, having said in his history that on the night Alexander was born the temple of Diana at Ephesus burned down, added that this was by no means to be wondered at, since Diana, having wished to be present at the childbed of Olympias, was absent from home. And the goddess who would come to all things our people named Venus, and rather charm (venustas) is from her than Venus from charm.

Nor indeed is the stage alone filled with these crimes, but common life with far greater. The house of each man feels it, the forum feels it, the senate-house, the field, the allies, the provinces feel it — that, as right is done by reason, so by reason wrong is done; and the one both by few and rarely, the other both always and by very many; so that it would have been better that no reason at all had been given us by the immortal gods than that it should have been given with so great ruin. As wine, because it rarely profits the sick, very often harms them, it is better not to administer it at all than to run into open ruin in hope of a doubtful cure; so I am not sure whether it had not been better for the human race that that swift motion of thought, that keenness, that cunning, which we call reason, since it is pernicious to very many and wholesome to very few, should not have been given at all than given so munificently and so largely.

To say this is more shameful than to be unable to defend what he wished to maintain. The same he does against the logicians; for whereas they have handed down that in all disjunctions in which "either yes or no" is set, one or the other is true, he feared that, if anything of this kind were granted — "Epicurus will either be alive tomorrow or will not" — one or the other would become necessary; and so he denied that the whole "either yes or no" was necessary: than which what could be said more obtuse? Arcesilas pressed Zeno, since he himself said that all things that appeared to the senses were false, while Zeno said some appearances were false, not all; Epicurus feared that, if one appearance were false, none would be true: he said that all the senses are messengers of the truth. Nothing of these is anything but the height of folly; for he was receiving a heavier blow in order to ward off a lighter.

Do you see, then, how the reasoning, drawn from natural things well and usefully discovered, has been carried over to invented and fictitious gods? Which thing has begotten false opinions and turbulent errors and superstitions almost of old wives. For both the forms of the gods, and their ages, and their dress and adornment are known to us, their families besides, their marriages, their kinships, and all things brought down to the likeness of human weakness. For they are even brought in with troubled minds: for we have received the desires of the gods, their sicknesses, their fits of anger; nor indeed, as the fables tell, were they without wars and battles — not only as in Homer, when different gods defended two opposing armies from different sides, but even when they waged their own proper wars, as with the Titans, as with the Giants. These things are both told and believed most foolishly, and are full of futility and the height of triviality.

Wherefore, if the divine mind and will took thought for men on this ground, that it bestowed reason on them, it took thought for those alone on whom it bestowed good reason — whom, if there are any at all, we see to be very few. But it does not please us that the immortal gods took thought for a few; it follows, then, that they took thought for no one. To this point you are wont to meet thus: that it is not therefore not best provided for us by the gods because many use their benefit perversely; that many use their patrimonies ill too, and not for that cause have no benefit from their fathers. Who denies that? Or what likeness is there in that comparison? For Deianira did not wish to harm Hercules when she gave him the tunic dyed with the Centaur's blood, nor did he who with the sword opened the abscess of Jason of Pherae, which the physicians could not cure, wish to benefit him. For many have profited even when they wished to harm, and harmed when they wished to profit; so it does not follow from what is given that the will of him who gave it appears, nor, if he who received it uses it well, did he who gave it therefore give it in friendship. For what lust, what avarice, what crime is either undertaken without counsel taken, or, without motion and thought of the mind, brought to its end by reason?

The same he does in the matter of the nature of the gods: while he avoids the concretion of indivisible bodies, lest destruction and dispersal follow, he denies that the body of the gods is body but as it were body, and that there is blood but as it were blood. It seems a wonder that one soothsayer does not laugh when he sees another; is this not more of a wonder, that you can keep from laughing among yourselves? It is not body but as it were body: I should understand what that meant if it were modelled in wax or in clay figures; but in a god what "as it were body" or what "as it were blood" may be I cannot understand. Nor can you, Velleius — but you will not own it.

Yet, those fables despised and rejected, a god pervading the nature of each thing — through the lands Ceres, through the seas Neptune, others through others — may be understood, who and of what kind they are, and by what name custom has named them. These gods we ought both to revere and to worship. And the worship of the gods is best, and likewise most chaste, most holy, and most full of piety, that we should always revere them with a mind and a voice pure, whole, and uncorrupted. For not only the philosophers but our forefathers too separated superstition from religion.

For every opinion is reason, and indeed good reason if the opinion is true, but bad if it is false. But from god we have only reason, if indeed we have it; but good reason or not good is from ourselves. For reason was not given to man by the gods' benefit as a patrimony is left; for what rather would the gods have given to men if they had wished to harm them? And what would be the seeds of injustice, of intemperance, of cowardice, if reason did not underlie these vices? Medea and Atreus were just now mentioned by us, heroic persons plotting wicked crimes by reckoning taken and cast up.

For these things are given back by you as if dictated — things which Epicurus, yawning, babbled in a dream, though indeed he boasted, as we see in his writings, that he had no master. This I could readily believe even were he not to proclaim it, just as a man with a badly built house might boast that he had had no architect; for there is no smell of the Academy about him, none of the Lyceum, none even of the boys' schoolroom. He might have heard Xenocrates (and what a man, ye immortal gods!), and there are some who think he did; he himself denies it — I believe him, for he would not own a debt to anyone. He says he heard at Samos a certain Pamphilus, a pupil of Plato (for there as a young man he lived with his father and brothers, his father Neocles having gone there as a settler, but, since the little farm did not feed him sufficiently, I suppose, he was a schoolmaster);

For those who used to pray and sacrifice whole days that their children might survive (superstites) them were called superstitious — a name which afterwards spread more widely; while those who diligently handled over again, and as it were re-read (relegerent), all that pertained to the worship of the gods were called religious from re-reading (ex relegendo), as elegant (elegantes) from choosing (ex eligendo), as diligent (diligentes) from being careful (ex diligendo), as intelligent (intellegentes) from understanding (ex intellegendo); for in all these words there is the same force of 'choosing' (legendi) which there is in 'religious.' So it came about that of 'superstitious' and 'religious' the one became a name of fault, the other of praise. And I think I have sufficiently shown both that the gods exist and of what kind they are.

What of the trivialities of comedy — are they not always engaged in reason? Does not that fellow in the Eunuch argue subtly enough: 'What, then, shall I do? She has shut me out, she calls me back; shall I return? Not if she should beseech me.' And that one in the Comrades, after the manner of the Academics, does not hesitate to fight with reason against the common opinion, who says that 'in the height of love and the height of want it is pleasant' to have a father avaricious, ungracious toward his children, harsh, who neither loves you nor is zealous for you; and to this incredible opinion he supplies his little reasons:

but this Platonist Epicurus despises wonderfully: so afraid is he ever to seem to have learned anything. As for Nausiphanes the Democritean, he is caught fast: him he does not deny that he heard, yet he harasses with every kind of abuse. And yet, if he had not heard these doctrines of Democritus, what had he heard? What is there in Epicurus's natural philosophy that is not from Democritus? For though he changed some things, such as what I said a little while ago about the swerve of the atoms, yet he says most things the same: atoms, void, images, the infinity of spaces, the innumerability of worlds, their births and deaths — well-nigh everything in which the theory of nature is contained. Now this "as it were body" and "as it were blood" of yours — what do you understand by it?

The next thing is for me to show that the world is administered by the providence of the gods. A great topic indeed, and one assailed by your school, Cotta, and assuredly all the contest is with you. For to you, Velleius, it is less known how each thing is stated; for you read only your own writings, love your own, and condemn the rest with the case unheard. Thus you yourself said yesterday that a soothsaying old woman, Pronoia, that is, Providence, is brought in by the Stoics. You said this by that error, because you suppose that Providence is feigned by them as a kind of single goddess who governs and rules the whole world.

'either you may cheat him of his gain, or by letters divert some debt, or by a little slave frighten him in his fear; in short, what you take from a stingy father, how much more gladly you squander it!' And the same fellow argues that a father easy and liberal is a hindrance to a son in love: 'whom I know not in any way how to cheat, nor what to carry off from him, nor what trick or contrivance to set in motion against him: so has the obligingness of my father baffled all my tricks, deceits, jugglings.' What, then, of those tricks, those contrivances, those deceits and jugglings — could they have been without reason? O glorious gift of the gods! that Phormio could say: 'Bring me the old man; all my counsels are now drawn up in my heart.' But let us go out of the theatre, let us come into the forum.

For I not only confess but readily allow that you know these matters better than I; yet, once they have been stated, what is there that Velleius can understand and Cotta cannot? And so I understand what body is, what blood is, but "as it were body" and "as it were blood" I understand in no way at all. Nor do you hide it from me as Pythagoras was wont to hide things from strangers, nor do you speak obscurely on purpose like Heraclitus; but — between ourselves be it said — you yourself do not understand it either.

But this is said elliptically: just as, if anyone says that the commonwealth of the Athenians is ruled by the counsel of the Areopagus, the word 'of the Areopagus' is omitted; so, when we say that the world is administered by providence, judge that the word 'of the gods' is wanting, and reckon that it is fully and completely said thus: that the world is administered by the providence of the gods. So that wit, which your tribe lacks, do not spend in mocking us; and, by Hercules, if you would listen to me, do not even attempt it; it does not become you, it has not been given you, you cannot do it. Nor indeed does this apply to you alone, polished by domestic manners and the urbanity of our countrymen, but to the rest of your school, and most of all to him who begot these doctrines — a man without art, without letters, insolent toward all, without any keenness, without authority, without charm.

The praetor goes to take his seat. To judge what? Who has set fire to the record-office. What crime more hidden? But Quintus Sosius, a brilliant Roman knight from the Picene country, confessed that he had done it. Who has falsified the public records? That too Lucius Alenus did, when he imitated the handwriting of the six chief clerks; what more cunning than this man? Mark other inquiries — of the Tolosan gold, of the Jugurthine conspiracy; recall earlier ones — of Tubulus, about money taken for giving judgement; later ones — of incest, by the Peducaean bill; then these everyday ones — of the dagger, of poisons, of embezzlement, and, by a new law, even inquiries about wills. Hence that action, 'I say a theft was committed by your help and counsel'; hence so many judgements about bad faith — of guardianship, of mandate, of partnership, of trust — and the rest which are done against good faith out of buying or selling or hiring or letting; hence the public judgement of a private matter by the Laetorian law; hence that broom of all knaveries, the judgement concerning evil fraud, which our friend Gaius Aquillius brought forward — which fraud the same Aquillius holds to be present when one thing is pretended and another done.

This I see you contending for: that there is a kind of appearance of the gods which has nothing concrete, nothing solid, nothing pressed out, nothing prominent, but is pure, light, and transparent. We shall say, then, the same as of the Venus of Cos: that yonder is not body but the likeness of body, and that the spreading red mingled with white is not blood but a kind of likeness of blood; so in the Epicurean god there is not the thing but the likenesses of things. Suppose me persuaded of that which cannot even be understood: come, give me the outlines and shapes of these shadowy gods of yours.

I say, then, that the world, and all the parts of the world, were both established in the beginning and are at all times administered by the providence of the gods. And this discourse our school commonly divides into three parts. The first is that which is drawn from the reasoning which teaches that the gods exist; which granted, it must be confessed that the world is administered by their counsel. The second is that which teaches that all things are subject to a sentient Nature, and that all things are most beautifully governed by it; which established, it follows that it was generated from living principles. The third topic is that which is drawn from the wonder of things heavenly and earthly.

Do we think, then, that this great sowing of evils was made by the immortal gods? For if the gods gave reason to men, they gave malice; for malice is a crafty and deceitful reasoning of doing harm; the gods likewise gave fraud, crime, and the rest, of which none can either be undertaken without reason or accomplished. Would, then, that — as that old woman wishes the fir-beams had not fallen to the ground, cut by axes in the grove of Pelion — the gods had not given men that cunning, which very few use well, who yet themselves are often oppressed by those who use it ill, while innumerable use it wickedly; so that this divine gift of reason and counsel seems to have been imparted to men for fraud, not for goodness.

Here you are not without an abundance of arguments by which you would teach that the gods are of human form: first, because it is so shaped and anticipated in our minds that, when a man thinks of god, the human form presents itself; next, because, since the divine nature excels all things, it ought also to be of the most beautiful form, and none is more beautiful than the human; you bring forward a third argument, that in no other shape can mind have its dwelling.

First, then, either it must be denied that the gods exist — which both Democritus, by bringing in his 'phantoms' (simulacra), and Epicurus, by bringing in his 'images' (imagines), in a manner deny — or those who grant that the gods exist must confess that they do something, and that something glorious; but there is nothing more glorious than the administration of the world; therefore it is administered by the counsel of the gods. But if it is otherwise, there must assuredly be something better and endowed with greater force than god, whatever it be, whether an inanimate nature or a necessity driven by great force, producing these most beautiful works which we behold;

But you press again and again that this is the fault of men, not of the gods. As if a physician should blame the gravity of the disease, a pilot the force of the storm; even these, indeed, are poor mortals, yet ridiculous: 'for who would have called you in,' one might say, 'if these things did not exist?' Against god one may argue more freely: 'You say the fault is in the vices of men: you should have given men that reason which would have shut out vices and fault.' Where, then, was there room for an error of the gods? For we leave our patrimonies in hope of handing them on well, in which we may be deceived; but how could god be deceived? Or as the Sun when he took up his son Phaethon into his car, or Neptune when Theseus destroyed Hippolytus, having got from his father Neptune the power of wishing thrice?

Consider, then, each of these in turn, of what kind it is; for you seem to me to snatch up, as if by your own right, a thing in no way to be approved. First of all, who was ever so blind in contemplating things as not to see that those human forms have been transferred to the gods either by some design of wise men, that they might the more easily turn the minds of the ignorant from depravity of life to the worship of the gods, or by superstition, so that there might be images which worshippers believed they approached the very gods themselves? And the poets, painters, and craftsmen increased this same notion; for it was not easy to keep the gods, who are represented as doing and contriving something, in the imitation of other forms. There came in also this opinion, perhaps, that nothing seems to man more beautiful than man. But do you not see, as a natural philosopher, how flattering a match-maker, how, as it were, her own pander, Nature is? Do you think there is any beast on land or sea that does not take most delight in a beast of its own kind? If it were not so, why would not a bull be eager for the embrace of a mare, or a horse of a cow? Do you think an eagle, or a lion, or a dolphin prefers any shape to its own? What wonder, then, if in this same way Nature has prescribed to man that he should think nothing more beautiful than man? That is the reason why we suppose the gods like men: what do you think — if there were reason in the beasts, would they not each have assigned the most to their own kind?

the nature of the gods, then, is not all-powerful nor pre-eminent, if indeed it is subject to that necessity or nature by which sky, seas, and lands are ruled. But nothing is more excellent than god; therefore the world must of necessity be ruled by him; the god, therefore, is obedient or subject to no nature; he himself, then, rules all nature. For if we grant that the gods are intelligent, we grant also that they are provident, and of the greatest matters indeed. Do they, then, not know what matters are greatest, and in what way they are to be handled and watched over; or have they not the power to sustain and manage so great things? But both ignorance of things is foreign to the nature of the gods, and difficulty in sustaining their office through weakness by no means befalls the majesty of the gods. From which is brought about what we wish — that the world is administered by the providence of the gods.

These things are the poets'; but we wish to be philosophers, authors of facts not of fables. And yet these very poetic gods, if they had known those things would be pernicious to their sons, would be thought to have erred in their benefit. And if it is true what Aristo of Chios was wont to say — that the philosophers harm their hearers who interpret well-spoken things ill (for prodigals could come out of the school of Aristippus, sour men out of the school of Zeno) — then plainly, if those who had heard them were going to come away vicious, because they interpreted the philosophers' discourse perversely, it were better for the philosophers to be silent than to harm those who had heard them;

But, by Hercules, I (for I will speak as I feel), much as I love myself, do not dare to say that I am more beautiful than that bull was which carried off Europa; for the question here is not of our talents or our speeches but of appearance and shape. And if we wished to invent and join shapes for ourselves, like that sea Triton who is painted riding upon swimming beasts harnessed to a human body, you would not wish to be such a thing. I am on difficult ground; for so great is the force of Nature that no man would wish to be other than like a man — and indeed an ant like an ant.

And it must of necessity be that, since the gods exist (if indeed they do, as assuredly they do), they are living beings, and not only living but endowed with reason and joined together among themselves as it were by a civil bond and fellowship, ruling one world as a common commonwealth and a kind of city.

so, if men turn the reason given by the immortal gods with good intent to fraud and malice, it had been better for the human race that it not be given than that it be given. As, if a physician should know that a sick man who has been bidden to take wine will take it too strong and straightway perish, he would be greatly at fault, so that Providence of yours is to be blamed, which gave reason to those whom it knew would use it perversely and wickedly. Unless, perhaps, you say it did not know. Would indeed that you might! But you will not dare, for I am not ignorant how greatly you esteem its name.

But like what man? For how few are handsome! When I was at Athens, scarcely one was found in a whole troop of youths — I see why you smiled, but the matter stands so. Then to us, who, with the leave of the old philosophers, delight in young men, even faults are often pleasing. A mole on a boy's finger pleased Alcaeus; but a mole is a blemish of the body; yet to him it seemed a beauty. Quintus Catulus, the father of our colleague and friend, loved your townsman Roscius, and even wrote of him: "I had stood by chance saluting the rising Dawn, when suddenly on my left Roscius rose. By your leave, ye heavenly ones, may I say it: the mortal seemed fairer than the god." To him fairer than a god; yet he was, as he is today, of the most distorted eyes: what does it matter, if to him this very thing seemed witty and charming?

It follows that there is in them the same reason as in the human race, that the same truth is in both, and the same law, which is the prescribing of right and the repelling of wrong. From which it is understood that prudence too and mind have come to men from the gods (and for that cause, by the institutions of our forefathers, Mind, Faith, Virtue, Concord have been consecrated and publicly dedicated; for how is it fitting to deny that these are among the gods, when we revere their august and holy images? But if mind, faith, virtue, concord are in the race of men, whence could these have flowed to earth but from on high?), and since there are in us counsel, reason, prudence, the gods must of necessity have these very things greater, and not only have them but also use them in the greatest and best matters.

But this topic indeed can now be concluded. For if folly, by the consent of all philosophers, is a greater evil than if all the evils both of fortune and of the body were set on the other side, and yet no one attains wisdom, we are all in the greatest evils — we for whom you say it is best provided by the immortal gods. For as it makes no difference whether no one is well or no one can be well, so I do not understand what difference there is whether no one is wise or no one can be wise. But we are saying too much about a most manifest matter; while Telamon in one verse settles the whole topic, why the gods neglect men: 'For if they cared, it would be well with the good, ill with the bad; which now is not so.' They indeed ought to have made all men good, if they took thought for the human race;

I return to the gods. Do we think any of them — if not so cross-eyed, then at least with a cast — any with a mole, any snub-nosed, flap-eared, beetle-browed, or big-headed, as some among us are; or is everything corrected in them? Grant you that; is there also one face for all of them? For if there are several, one must be more beautiful than another, and so some god is not the most beautiful; if there is one face for all, then the Academy must flourish in heaven: for if there is no difference between god and god, among the gods there is no recognition, no perception.

But nothing is greater or better than the world; the world, therefore, must of necessity be administered by the counsel and providence of the gods. Finally, when we have sufficiently shown these to be gods whose marked force and brilliant aspect we behold — I mean the sun and moon, and the wandering and the fixed stars, and the sky, and the world itself, and the force of those things which are present in the whole world with great use and advantage to the human race — it is brought about that all things are ruled by a divine mind and prudence. And of the first part enough has been said.

but if that less, at least they ought to have taken thought for the good. Why, then, did the Carthaginian crush in Spain the two Scipios, bravest and best of men; why did Maximus bury his son, a man of consular rank; why did Hannibal slay Marcellus; why did Cannae carry off Paulus; why was the body of Regulus given to the cruelty of the Carthaginians; why did his own household walls not shelter Africanus? But these are old, and very many others; let us look at nearer ones. Why is my uncle, a most blameless and most learned man, Publius Rutilius, in exile; why was my comrade Drusus slain in his own house; why was that pattern of temperance and prudence, Quintus Scaevola, the chief pontiff, butchered before the image of Vesta; why before that too were so many leading men of the state slain by Cinna; why could Gaius Marius, most treacherous of all, bid Quintus Catulus, a man of most excellent dignity, to die?

What if even that, Velleius, is altogether false — that no other appearance than man's presents itself to us when we think of god: will you still defend doctrines so absurd? To us perhaps it presents itself so, as you say; for from childhood we have known Jupiter, Juno, Minerva, Neptune, Vulcan, Apollo, and the rest of the gods by that face which painters and sculptors chose, and not only by face but by adornment, age, and dress. But not so the Egyptians, nor the Syrians, nor almost any of the barbarians; for you may see among them firmer opinions about certain beasts than among us about the most holy temples and images of the gods.

It follows that I should show that all things are subject to Nature, and that they are most beautifully governed by it. But what Nature itself is must first be briefly explained, that what we wish to show may the more easily be understood. For some hold that Nature is a certain force without reason that stirs up necessary motions in bodies; but others hold it to be a force partaking of reason and order, proceeding as it were by a method, and declaring what each thing's cause produces and what follows, whose skill no art, no hand, no craftsman can attain in imitating. For the force of a seed is so great that, although it is exceedingly small, yet, if it falls upon a nature that conceives and grasps it, and gets hold of material by which it can be nourished and increased, it so fashions and produces each thing in its own kind that some are nourished only through their own stems, while others can even move and feel and desire and beget from themselves things like themselves.

The day would fail me if I should wish to number those good men to whom it has gone ill, nor less if I should recall those wicked men to whom it has gone most well. For why did Marius, so happily consul for the seventh time, die an old man in his own house; why did Cinna, most cruel of all, reign so long? 'But he paid the penalty.' It had been better that he be hindered and prevented from slaying so many of the highest men than that he himself at last pay the penalty. With the utmost torment and punishment Quintus Varius, a most ruthless man, perished; if it was because he had cut off Drusus with the sword and Metellus with poison, it had been better that those be preserved than that Varius pay the penalty of his crime. The tyrant Dionysius was for eight-and-thirty years master of a most opulent and most prosperous state;

For we see many shrines despoiled and images of the gods carried off from the most sacred places by our own people; but it has never so much as been heard that a crocodile, or an ibis, or a cat was harmed by an Egyptian. What, then, do you think — does not Apis, that sacred bull of the Egyptians, seem a god to the Egyptians? Quite as much, by Hercules, as that Saviour-goddess of yours does to you. Whom you never see, even in dreams, save with a goatskin, a spear, a little shield, and upturned slippers. But such is not the Argive Juno, nor the Roman. Therefore Juno has one shape among the Argives, another among the people of Lanuvium. And indeed we have one Jupiter of the Capitol, the Africans another, Jupiter Hammon.

There are, however, some who call all things by the name of nature, like Epicurus, who divides thus: that the nature of all that exists is bodies and void and the things that befall these. But when we say that the world consists of, and is administered by, nature, we do not so speak as of a clod, or a fragment of stone, or anything of that kind, which has no nature of holding together, but as of a tree, as of a living creature, in which there is no rashness but order appears, and a kind of likeness of art.

how many before him, in the very flower of Greece, was Pisistratus! 'But Phalaris, but Apollodorus paid the penalty.' Yes, but after many had first been tortured and slain. And many robbers often pay the penalty, yet we cannot say that more captives have not been cruelly slain than robbers. We have heard that Anaxarchus the Democritean was tortured to death by the tyrant of Cyprus, that Zeno of Elea was slain amid torments; what shall I say of Socrates, over whose death I am wont to weep when I read Plato? Do you see, then, that, in the judgement of the gods, if they see human affairs, the distinction has been done away?

Is it not shameful, then, for a natural philosopher — that is, a spy and hunter of nature — to seek the witness of truth from minds steeped in habit? For in that way it will be allowed to say that Jupiter is always bearded, Apollo always beardless, that Minerva's eyes are grey, Neptune's blue. And indeed we praise the Vulcan at Athens which Alcamenes made, in which, as the god stands clothed, a slight, not unsightly limp appears: a lame god, then, we shall have, since we have received this of Vulcan. Come, and do we make the gods bear those very names by which we call them?

But if the things which are held in the earth by their stems live and flourish by the art of Nature, surely the earth itself is held together by the same force, by the art of Nature, since, made pregnant with seeds, it brings forth and pours out all things from itself, embraces the stems, nourishes and increases them, and is itself in turn nourished by the higher and external natures; and by its exhalations both the air and the ether and all things above are nourished. So, if the earth is held together and flourishes by nature, the same reasoning holds in the rest of the world; for the stems cling to the earth, while living creatures are sustained by the breathing of the air; and the air itself sees with us, hears with us, sounds with us, for none of these can be done without it; nay, it even moves with us, for wherever we go, wherever we move, it seems as it were to give place and yield.

Diogenes the Cynic, indeed, was wont to say that Harpalus, who in those days was held a fortunate robber, bore witness against the gods, because he lived so long in that fortune. Dionysius, of whom I spoke before, when he had plundered the shrine of Proserpina at Locri, was sailing to Syracuse; and when he held his course with a most favourable wind, laughing he said: 'Do you see, my friends, what a good voyage the immortal gods grant to the sacrilegious?' And the shrewd fellow, when he had perceived this well and plainly, persevered in the same opinion. When he had brought his fleet to the Peloponnese and had come into the shrine of Olympian Jove, he took off from him a golden cloak of great weight, with which the tyrant Gelo had adorned Jove out of the spoils of the Carthaginians, and even jested over it, that a golden cloak was heavy in summer and cold in winter, and threw over him a woollen mantle, saying that this was fit for every season of the year. The same man bade the golden beard of Aesculapius at Epidaurus be taken off; for it was not fitting, he said, that the son should be bearded when in all the shrines the father was beardless.

But first, as many as are the tongues of men, so many are the names of the gods. For Vulcan is not, as you, Velleius, the same wherever you go — the same in Italy, the same in Africa, the same in Spain. Next, the number of names is not great even in our pontifical books, while the gods are innumerable. Or are they without names? That indeed you must say; for what point is there, when the face is one, in there being several names? How much better it would have been, Velleius, to confess rather that you do not know what you do not know, than, blurting these things out, to feel sick at them and dissatisfied with yourself! Do you think a god is like me, or like you? Surely you do not. "What then? Shall I call the sun, or the moon, or the sky a god? Then also blessed: enjoying what pleasures? And wise: but how can there be wisdom in such a block?"

And the things which are borne to the middle place of the world, which is the lowest, and the things which from the middle are borne to the upper, and the things which are carried round about the middle in a circular revolution, make up the continuous world and one nature. And since there are four kinds of bodies, the nature of the world is made continuous by their interchange. For from earth arises water, from water air, from air ether; then, backward again in turn, from ether air, then water, from water the lowest earth. Thus, by the natures of which all things consist passing to and fro, up and down, this way and that, the conjunction of the parts of the world is held together.

Then he bade the silver tables be carried off from all the shrines, on which, since after the custom of old Greece there was inscribed 'belonging to the good gods,' he said he wished to make use of their goodness. The same man without hesitation took away the little golden Victories and the bowls and crowns which were held in the outstretched hands of the images, and said he was receiving, not carrying off, these things; for it was folly to be unwilling to take from those, holding them out and giving them, from whom we prayed for good things. And they say the same man brought out these things which I have said, taken from the shrines, into the forum, and sold them by the crier, and, the money exacted, made proclamation that whatever anyone had of sacred things he should bring back, before a certain day, each to its own shrine: so to impiety toward the gods he joined injustice toward men. This man, then, neither did Olympian Jove smite with a thunderbolt nor did Aesculapius destroy, wasting away with a wretched and lingering disease; but he died in his own bed, was borne to the pyre as a tyrant, and the power which he himself had gotten by crime he handed on to his son as a just and lawful inheritance.

These are your doctrines. If, then, god is neither of human form, as I have shown, nor of some such other kind, as you are persuaded, why do you hesitate to deny that the gods exist? You do not dare. Wisely indeed, though here it is not the people you fear but the gods themselves. I have known Epicureans who worship every little image. Yet I see that to some it seems that Epicurus, lest he should fall under the displeasure of the Athenians, left the gods in word but did away with them in fact. And so in those choice and brief maxims of his which you call Kyriai Doxai, this, I think, is the first: "That which is blessed and immortal neither has trouble itself nor causes it to another."

And this must of necessity be either everlasting, in this same adornment which we see, or at least very long-lasting, enduring for a far and almost measureless time. And whichever of these be the case, it follows that the world is administered by Nature. For what voyaging of fleets, or what marshalling of an army, or, again, to compare the things which Nature produces, what generation of a vine or a tree, what shape of a living creature, or framing of its limbs, signifies so great a skill of Nature as the world itself? Either, then, there is nothing that is ruled by a sentient nature, or it must be confessed that the world is ruled.

Unwillingly does the discourse dwell on this point, for it seems to lend authority to sinning; and rightly would it seem so, were there not, even without any divine reason, the heavy weight of conscience itself, both of virtue and of vices, which taken away, all lies in ruins. For as neither a house nor a commonwealth would seem ordered by any reason and discipline, if in it there were no rewards for things rightly done and no punishments for sins, so there is assuredly no divine governance of the world over men, if in it there is no distinction between the good and the bad.

In this maxim, as it is set forth, there are some who think that what he did from plain unskilfulness in speaking he did on purpose. They do him an injustice, a man by no means cunning; for it is doubtful whether he says that something is blessed and immortal, or that, if anything is such, it is of this kind. They do not notice that here he spoke ambiguously, but in many other places both he and Metrodorus spoke as openly as you did a little while ago. He, however, does think the gods exist; nor have I ever seen anyone who feared more the things he said were not to be feared — death, I mean, and the gods: by which ordinary men are not so very greatly moved, yet of these he cries out that the minds of all mortals are terrified. So many thousands turn to brigandage with death set before them; others plunder all the shrines they can: I suppose the fear of death drives the one, the fear of religion the other. But since you do not dare (for now I will speak with Epicurus himself) to deny that the gods exist, what is there to hinder you from setting either the sun, or the world, or some everlasting mind among the number of the gods?

For how can that which contains all the other natures and their seeds be itself not administered by Nature? — just as, if anyone should say that teeth and the growth of manhood come into being by nature, but that the man himself in whom these come into being does not consist by nature, he would not understand that the things which put forth something out of themselves have more perfect natures than the things which are put forth from them. But of all the things that are administered by Nature, the sower, the begetter, the parent, so to speak, the rearer and nourisher is the world; and it nurses and holds together all things as its members and parts. But if the parts of the world are administered by Nature, the world itself must of necessity be administered by Nature. Whose administration, indeed, has in it nothing that can be censured; for out of those natures which existed, what could best be produced has been produced.

'But the gods neglect lesser things, and do not pursue the little fields of individuals nor their little vines, and, if blight or hail has harmed anyone, that was not for Jove to take notice of; not even in their kingdoms do kings care for all the least things': for so you say. As if I had a little while ago complained about the Formian farm of Publius Rutilius and not about his lost welfare. And this indeed all mortals so hold — that external conveniences, vineyards, crops, olive-groves, the abundance of fruits and produce, in short every convenience and prosperity of life, they have from the gods; but virtue no one ever ascribed as received from a god.

"I never saw," he says, "a soul partaking of reason and counsel in any but the human shape." What — did you ever see anything like the sun, or the moon, or the five wandering stars? The sun, bounding his motion within the two extreme points of a single orbit, completes his yearly courses; the moon, kindled by his rays, fills out this same circuit in a month's space; while the five stars, keeping the same orbit, some nearer the earth, some farther, from the same starting-points complete the same spaces in unequal times. Did you, Epicurus, ever see anything like this?

Let someone, then, show that it could have been done better; but no one will ever show it, and if anyone shall wish to correct anything, he will either make it worse or will be longing for what could not have been done. But if all the parts of the world are so constituted that they could be neither better for use nor more beautiful for appearance, let us see whether these things are fortuitous, or in such a state that they could in no way cohere save under the direction of sense and divine providence. If, then, those things which Nature has perfected are better than those which art has, and art makes nothing without reason, neither must Nature be held void of reason. How is it fitting, then, that when you behold a statue or a painted tablet you know that art has been employed, and when you see from afar the course of a ship you doubt not that it is moved by reason and art, and when you look upon a sundial, whether marked out or worked by water, you understand that the hours are shown by art and not by chance, yet you think the world, which embraces these very arts and their craftsmen and all things, to be void of counsel and reason?

And rightly, no doubt; for on account of virtue we are justly praised and in virtue rightly glory; which would not happen if we had it as a gift from a god, not from ourselves. But indeed, when we are increased in honours, or in estate, or if we have gotten any other fortuitous good or driven off an evil, then we give thanks to the gods, then we think nothing added to our own praise. Did anyone ever give thanks to the gods because he was a good man? But because he was rich, because honoured, because safe; and they call Jove best and greatest on account of these things, not because he makes us just, temperate, wise, but because safe, sound, opulent, well-supplied;

Let there be, then, no sun, no moon, no stars, since nothing can exist but what we have touched or seen. What — have you yourself seen god? Why, then, do you believe he exists? Let us, on this reasoning, do away with everything that either history or some new reasoning brings us. So it comes about that the men of the interior do not believe there is a sea. What narrowness of mind is this — that, if you had been born in Seriphos and had never gone out of the island, where you had often seen little hares and foxes, you would not believe there were lions and panthers when you were told what they were like; and if anyone spoke to you of an elephant, you would think you were even being laughed at?

But if anyone should carry into Scythia or Britain that sphere which our friend Posidonius lately made, whose single revolutions bring about the same in the sun and in the moon and in the five wandering stars as is brought about in the heaven on single days and nights, who in that barbarous land would doubt that that sphere had been perfected by reason? Yet these men doubt about the world, from which all things arise and come to be, whether it has been brought about by chance or by some necessity, or by reason and a divine mind; and they think Archimedes had more power in imitating the revolutions of the sphere than Nature in producing them — especially when those revolutions were perfected with far more skill than these were copied.

nor did anyone ever vow a tenth to Hercules if he should be made wise — although Pythagoras, when he had discovered something new in geometry, is said to have sacrificed an ox to the Muses; but that indeed I do not believe, since he was unwilling to sacrifice a victim even to Apollo at Delos, lest he should sprinkle the altar with blood. But, to return to the point, this is the judgement of all mortals — that fortune is to be sought from god, but wisdom to be taken from oneself. Although we may consecrate shrines to Mind and to Virtue and to Faith, yet we see these placed in ourselves; the means of hope, of safety, of help, of victory must be sought from the gods. The prosperity and good fortune of the wicked, therefore, refute, as Diogenes said, all the force and power of the gods.

And you, Velleius, have wound up your opinion not in your school's manner but in the cramped argument of the logicians, a tribe your school has never come to know. You assumed that the gods are blessed: we grant it. That no one can be blessed without virtue: that too we give, and gladly. That virtue cannot subsist without reason: that too must be agreed. You add that there is no reason save in the human shape. Who, do you think, will grant you this? For if it were so, what need was there for you to arrive there step by step? You might have assumed it by your own right. But what is this "step by step"? For I see you have come by degrees from the blessed to virtue, from virtue to reason; but from reason to the human shape, how do you proceed? That is to fall headlong, not to step down.

And as that shepherd in Accius, who had never before seen a ship, when from a mountain he beheld afar the divine and strange vessel of the Argonauts, at first wondering and terrified speaks in this wise: 'So vast a mass glides roaring from the deep with mighty din and breath: it rolls the waves before it, by force whirls up eddies, plunges headlong, drenches the sea, blows it back; so that now you would believe a broken storm-cloud is rolling, now that some rock, driven by the winds or by tempests, is being snatched aloft, or that round whirlwinds are arising, struck by the clashing waves — unless the sea is stirring up some wreck of the land, or perhaps Triton, overturning with his trident the caverns beneath the very roots, heaves from the depths a mass of rock to the sky in the surging strait': at first he doubts what that nature is which he beholds unknown; and the same man, when the youths are seen and the sailors' song is heard, says, 'Like swift and eager dolphins snorting with their snouts' — and much else besides — that the song is borne to his ears like to the melody of Silvanus —

'But sometimes the good have good ends.' Those indeed we seize upon and ascribe, without any reason, to the immortal gods. But Diagoras, that one who is called the Atheist, when he had come to Samothrace, and a certain friend said to him: 'You, who think the gods neglect human things — do you not observe, from so many painted tablets, how many have escaped the force of the storm by their vows and come safe into harbour?' said: 'So it is; for those are nowhere painted who suffered shipwreck and perished at sea.' And the same man, when, as he was sailing, the passengers in an adverse storm, timid and terrified, told him that this had befallen them not unjustly, since they had taken him aboard the same ship, showed them in the same course many others labouring, and asked whether they believed Diagoras was being carried in those ships too. For so the matter stands, that toward prosperous or adverse fortune it makes no difference what kind of man you are, or how you have lived.

Nor indeed do I understand why Epicurus preferred to say that the gods are like men rather than that men are like the gods. You will ask what the difference is; for if this is like that, that is like this. I see; but this I say: that the figure of their form did not come to the gods from men. For the gods always existed and were never born, if indeed they are to be eternal; but men were born; therefore the human form existed before men, and the immortal gods were of that form: it is not, then, the gods' form that is to be called human, but ours divine. But this, indeed, as you please; this I ask, what so great fortune there was (for you will have nothing in the nature of things

so, as he at first sight thinks he beholds some lifeless thing void of sense, but afterwards, by surer signs, begins to suspect what kind of thing it is about which he had doubted, thus the philosophers ought, if perchance the first sight of the world had confounded them, afterwards, when they had seen its motions bounded and even, and all things governed by fixed orders and unchangeable constancy, to have understood that there is in this heavenly and divine house not only an inhabitant but a ruler and governor, and as it were the architect of so great a work and so great a charge. But as it is, they seem to me not even to suspect how great is the wonder of things heavenly and earthly.

'The gods,' he says, 'do not take note of all things, not even kings.' What is the likeness? For if kings knowingly pass things over, it is a great fault; but for god there is not even the excuse of ignorance. Whom you defend gloriously, when you say that the power of the gods is such that, even if anyone has escaped the penalties of his crime by death, those penalties are demanded of his children, grandchildren, and descendants. O wonderful equity of the gods! Would any state endure a proposer of a law of this kind, that a son or grandson should be condemned if a father or grandfather had offended? 'What end will be set to the slaughter of the house of Tantalus, or what satiety of punishment will ever be given, for the death of Myrtilus, by paying penalties?' Whether the poets have corrupted the Stoics, or the Stoics have lent authority to the poets, I could not easily say;

done by reason) — but yet what so great chance, whence so happy a concourse of atoms, that men should suddenly be born in the form of the gods? Are we to think that seeds of the gods fell from heaven upon the earth, and that thus men arose like their fathers? I could wish you said so; I would not unwillingly acknowledge kinship with the gods. You say nothing of the kind, but that it came about by chance that we are like the gods. And now arguments must be sought by which this may be refuted. Would that I could find the true as easily as I can confute the false! For you have recounted from memory and at length — so that it pleased me to wonder that there should be in a Roman so great a learning — the opinions of the philosophers concerning the nature of the gods, from Thales of Miletus onward.

For in the beginning the earth, set in the middle part of the world, is surrounded on every side by this living and breathable nature whose name is air — that word indeed is Greek, but yet has now been received into use by our people; for it is worn smooth as if it were Latin. This in turn is embraced by the boundless ether, which consists of the highest fires (let us borrow this word too, and let ether be said in Latin as air is, though Pacuvius interprets it: 'This which I speak of our people call sky, the Greeks ether' — as though, forsooth, it were not a Greek who says this. 'But he speaks Latin.' Yes, if indeed we do not hear him as one speaking Greek; for the same poet teaches in another place,

for portents and shameful things are said by both. For neither did he whom the iambic of Hipponax had wounded, or who was hurt by the verse of Archilochus, contain a grief sent in by a god and not conceived by himself; nor, when we see the lust of Aegisthus or that of Paris, do we ask a cause sent by a god, when we almost hear the voice of guilt itself; nor do I judge the health of many sick men to have been given rather by Hippocrates than by Aesculapius; nor shall I ever say that the discipline of the Lacedaemonians was given to Sparta by Apollo rather than by Lycurgus. Critolaus, I say, overthrew Corinth, Hasdrubal Carthage; these two men gouged out those eyes of the sea-coast — not some angry god, whom you say cannot be angry at all.

Did all those seem to you to be raving who decreed that god can subsist without hands and feet? Does not even this move you, when you consider what use and what fitness there is in the limbs of man, to judge that the gods have no need of human limbs? For what need is there of feet without walking, of hands if there is nothing to be grasped, of the whole disposition of all the parts of the body, in which there is nothing idle, nothing without cause, nothing superfluous, so that no art can imitate the skill of Nature? Will god, then, have a tongue and not speak, teeth, palate, throat, to no use, and the parts which Nature has joined to the body for the sake of procreation — these too will god have to no purpose; nor the outer parts more than the inner, the heart, lungs, liver, and the rest — which, their usefulness taken away, what beauty have they (since you would have these to be in god for the sake of beauty)?

'Greek-born — the speech itself reveals it' from yonder line) — but let us return to greater things. From the ether, then, arise the innumerable flames of the heavenly bodies, of which the chief is the sun, lighting up all things with the clearest light, many times greater and ampler than the whole earth; then the rest of the heavenly bodies, of measureless magnitudes. And these fires, so great and so many, not only do no harm to the earth and earthly things, but so benefit them that, if they were moved from their place, the earth must inevitably be burned up by such fires, all moderation and tempering being removed.

But surely a god could have come to their aid and preserved cities so great and so noble; for you yourselves are wont to say that there is nothing which a god cannot do, and that without any toil; for as the limbs of men are moved by the mind itself and the will with no effort, so by the will of the gods all things can be fashioned, moved, and changed. And this you say not superstitiously and like old wives, but with a physical and consistent reasoning; for you say that the matter of things, out of which and in which all things are, is wholly flexible and changeable, so that there is nothing which cannot, however suddenly, be fashioned and changed out of it, but that the fashioner and governor of this universal matter is divine providence; this, then, whithersoever it moves itself, can bring about whatever it will. And so either it does not know what it can do, or it neglects human affairs, or it cannot judge what is best.

Trusting in these dreams, not only Epicurus, Metrodorus, and Hermarchus spoke against Pythagoras, Plato, and Empedocles, but even the little courtesan Leontium dared to write against Theophrastus — in choice and Attic style, to be sure, but yet she did: so much licence did the Garden of Epicurus possess. And yet you are wont to complain; Zeno indeed even went to law. Why should I speak of Albucius? As for Phaedrus, nothing was more elegant, nothing more humane, yet the old man was vexed if I said anything too harsh — while Epicurus assailed Aristotle most insultingly, spoke most foully of Phaedo the disciple of Socrates, cut to pieces in whole volumes Timocrates, the brother of his comrade Metrodorus, because he disagreed on some point of philosophy, was ungrateful to Democritus himself, whom he followed, and treated so ill Nausiphanes his master, from whom he had learned not a little. Zeno, indeed, not only stung with abuse those of his own time — Apollodorus, Sillis, and the rest — but even said that Socrates himself, the parent of philosophy, was, using a Latin word, an Attic buffoon, and never called Chrysippus anything but Chrysippa.

Here am I to wonder that there is any man who persuades himself that certain solid and indivisible bodies are borne along by force and weight, and that out of the fortuitous concourse of those bodies a world most adorned and most beautiful is made? He who thinks this could have come to pass, I do not see why he should not also think that, if innumerable forms of the one-and-twenty letters, whether of gold or of any kind you please, were thrown together somewhere, the Annals of Ennius could be produced out of them, cast upon the ground, so that they could be read straight through; whereas I doubt whether chance could avail so far even in a single verse.

'It does not care for individual men.' No wonder: not even for states; not for these: not even for nations and peoples. But if it will despise even these, what wonder is it that the whole human race has been despised by it? But how, while you say the same — that the gods do not pursue all things — do you also will that dreams be distributed and divided among men by the immortal gods (this I say to you because it is your school's opinion about the truth of dreams), and also say that vows ought to be undertaken? For individuals make vows; the divine mind, then, hears even concerning individuals; you see, then, that it is not so occupied as you thought. Grant that it is stretched out, turning the sky, watching the earth, governing the seas: why does it suffer so many gods to do nothing and be idle? Why does it not set over human affairs some of those idle gods who were unfolded by you, Balbus, in numbers innumerable? These things, in the main, I had to say about the nature of the gods, not that I might do away with it, but that you might understand how obscure it is and how difficult its explanations have." When he had said this, Cotta ended.

You yourself a little while ago, when you recited, as it were, a senate of philosophers, said that the greatest of men doted, raved, were out of their minds. But if none of these saw the truth about the nature of the gods, it is to be feared that there is no nature of the gods at all. For these things which you say are wholly made up, scarcely worth the lamp-oil of little old women. For you do not perceive how much you must take upon yourselves, if you should win our concession that the form of men and of gods is the same. The whole care and tendance of the body that is bestowed upon a man will have to be bestowed upon a god — walking, running, reclining, leaning, sitting, grasping, and at the last even talk and speech.

But how do these men assert that the world has been perfected out of little bodies endowed with no colour, no quality (which the Greeks call poiotes), no sensation, but rushing together rashly and by chance — or rather that innumerable worlds, at every point of time, are some being born, some perishing? But if the concourse of atoms can make a world, why can it not make a portico, a temple, a house, a city, which are less laborious to make, and indeed many of them far easier? Certainly they prate so rashly about the world that to me they seem never to have looked up at this wonderful adornment of the heaven — which is the topic that comes next.

But Lucilius said: "Too vehemently, Cotta, have you indeed inveighed against that doctrine of the Stoics which has been most devoutly and most prudently established by them concerning the providence of the gods. But since evening is coming on, you will give us some day that we may argue against these things. For there is a contest between me and you for our altars and hearths, and for the temples and shrines of the gods, and for the walls of the city, which you pontiffs say are holy, and you gird the city more carefully with religion than with the walls themselves; which I judge it impious to forsake, so long indeed as I can breathe."

As for your saying that the gods are male and female, you see what follows. For my part I cannot sufficiently wonder whence that chief of yours came by these opinions. But you do not cease to cry out that this must be held fast: that god is blessed and immortal. Yet what stands in the way of his being blessed if he is not two-footed? Or that — whether it is to be called "beatitas" or "beatitudo" (both indeed harsh, but by use words must be softened by us) — but that, whatever it is, why can it not befall the sun, or this world, or some eternal mind void of figure and bodily limbs?

Excellently, then, Aristotle says: 'If there were men who had always dwelt beneath the earth, in good and well-lighted dwellings adorned with statues and paintings and furnished with all those things with which they abound who are thought happy, but who had never come out above the earth, yet had received by report and hearsay that there was some divinity and power of the gods; and if then, at some time, the jaws of the earth being opened, they could escape from those hidden seats into these regions which we inhabit and come forth: when suddenly they beheld the earth and seas and sky, when they had come to know the greatness of the clouds and the force of the winds, and had gazed upon the sun and come to know both its greatness and beauty and also its efficacy, in that it makes the day by pouring light over the whole sky, and when, after night had darkened the lands, they beheld the whole sky picked out and adorned with stars, and the changing lights of the moon, now waxing, now waning, and the risings and settings of all these, and their fixed and unchangeable courses through all eternity — when they beheld these things, they would assuredly judge both that the gods exist, and that these great works

Then said Cotta: "For my part I both wish to be refuted, Balbus, and chose rather to discuss the things I have argued than to pass judgement, and I know for certain that I can easily be overcome by you." "Doubtless," said Velleius, "who even thinks that dreams are sent to us by Jove — which yet are not so trivial as is the Stoics' discourse about the nature of the gods." When these things had been said, we parted thus: that to Velleius the discourse of Cotta seemed the truer, but to me that of Balbus seemed to incline more toward the likeness of truth.

You say nothing else but "I never saw a blessed sun or world." Why — did you ever see any world but this? You will say no. Why, then, did you dare to say that there are not six hundred thousand worlds but innumerable? "Reason taught it." Then will not reason teach you this also — that, when the most excellent nature is sought, and that blessed and eternal, which alone is the divine nature, just as we are surpassed by it in immortality, so we are surpassed by it in excellence of mind, and as in mind so in body? Why, then, when we are inferior in all else, are we equal in form? For human virtue came nearer to the likeness of the gods than the human figure.

are the works of the gods.' Thus far he. But let us think of darkness as great as that which once, by an eruption of the fires of Etna, is said to have darkened the neighbouring regions, so that for two days no man recognised a man; and yet, when on the third day the sun shone out, they seemed to themselves to have come to life again: but if this same thing should befall us out of eternal darkness, that we should suddenly behold the light, what an aspect of the sky would seem to us! But by daily continuance and the habit of the eyes our minds grow accustomed, and they neither wonder at, nor seek the reasons of, the things they always see — as though it were the novelty rather than the magnitude of things that ought to rouse us to search out their causes.

Can anything so childish be said (to press the same point a little longer) as if we should say that those kinds of beasts which are born in the Red Sea or in India do not exist?
