And yet not even the most inquisitive of men can, by searching, hear of so many things as there are that come to be on land, sea, marshes, and rivers; shall we deny that they exist because we have never seen them? But that very likeness which delights you most — how little it bears on the matter! Is not a dog like a wolf (and, as Ennius says, "How like to us, that foulest of beasts, the ape!"); yet the characters of each are unlike. None of the beasts is more sagacious than the elephant;

For who would call that man a man, who, when he has seen such fixed motions of the sky, such ordered courses of the stars, and all things so connected and fitted together among themselves, denies that there is any reason in these, and says that they come about by chance — things which, with how great counsel they are managed, we cannot attain by any counsel of our own? Or, when we see something moved by some mechanism, as a sphere, a clock, and very many other things, do we not doubt that those works are of reason; and yet, when we see the rushing of the heaven moved and turned round with wonderful speed, most constantly bringing about the yearly vicissitudes with the highest welfare and preservation of all things, do we doubt that these are done not only by reason but by an excellent and divine reason?

but for shape, what is more uncouth? I speak of beasts; but among men themselves, are there not, even with the most similar forms, unlike characters, and, with like characters, unlike shapes? For if once, Velleius, we take up this kind of argument, mark whither it creeps. You assumed that reason cannot reside save in the human shape; another will assume that it cannot save in an earthly being, save in one that has been born, save in one that has grown up, save in one that has learned, save in one that consists of soul and a body frail and weak, in short, save in a man and a mortal. But if you stand against all these, why does shape alone confound you? For when all those things which I have set forth are added, you saw that there is reason and mind in man; with these taken away, you say you nevertheless know god, so long as the outlines remain. This is not to consider, but as it were to draw lots, what you say.

For now, the subtlety of arguing laid aside, we may in a manner contemplate with our eyes the beauty of those things which we say have been established by divine providence. And first let the whole earth be beheld, set in the middle seat of the world, solid and globular, gathered on every side into itself by its own inclinations, clad with flowers, herbs, trees, crops, of all which the incredible multitude is set off with an insatiable variety. Add to this the cool perennity of springs, the translucent waters of rivers, the greenest clothing of the banks, the hollow depths of caverns, the roughness of the rocks, the heights of overhanging mountains, and the immensities of the plains; add also the hidden veins of gold and silver and the boundless store of marble.

Unless perhaps you do not even attend to this — that not only in man but even in a tree whatever is superfluous or has no use is a hindrance. How troublesome it is to have one finger more than usual! Why so? Because the five neither need nor have use for another in respect of appearance or service. But your god is overstocked not with one finger only, but with head, neck, shoulders, sides, belly, back, knees, hands, feet, thighs, legs. If it is that he may be immortal, what have these limbs to do with life, what the face itself? Rather those — the brain, heart, lungs, liver: for these are the seats of life; the cast of the countenance has nothing to do with the maintenance of life.

And what and how varied are the kinds of beasts, whether tame or wild, what the gliding flights and songs of birds, what the pasturing of cattle, what the life of the woodland creatures! What, now, shall I say of the race of men, who, set as it were to till the earth, suffer it neither to be made savage by the brutishness of beasts nor laid waste by the roughness of plants, and by whose works the fields, islands, and shores shine, picked out with dwellings and cities? If we could behold these things with our eyes as with our minds, no one, gazing on the whole earth, would doubt of a divine reason.

And you blamed those who, from works grand and glorious — when they had beheld the world itself, its members the sky, lands, and seas, and the chief ornaments of these, the sun, moon, and stars, and when they had come to know the ripenings, changes, and vicissitudes of the seasons — suspected that there was some surpassing and excellent nature which had made these things, and moved, ruled, and governed them. These men, even if they wander from the truth in their conjecture, yet I see what they are following: but you, what great and notable work have you that seems wrought by a divine mind, from which you suspect the gods to exist? "I had," you say, "a certain idea of god implanted in my mind." And of a bearded Jupiter, too, and a helmeted Minerva: do you, then, think them such?

But again, how great is the beauty of the sea, what the aspect of the whole, what the multitude and variety of islands, what the loveliness of the coasts and shores, how many and how diverse the kinds of beasts, some submerged, some floating and swimming, some clinging to the rocks by their own shells! And the sea itself, so reaching toward the land, sports along the shores, so that it seems one nature blended of two.

How much better in this the unlearned multitude, who give to god not only the limbs of man but also the use of his limbs; for they give him bow, arrows, spear, shield, trident, thunderbolt; and though they do not see what the actions of the gods are, yet they cannot conceive a god doing nothing at all. Even the Egyptians, who are mocked, consecrated no beast save for some usefulness which they got from it; the ibises, for instance, destroy a great host of serpents, being tall birds with stiff legs and a horny, long beak; they ward off pestilence from Egypt when they kill and consume the winged snakes borne in from the wastes of Libya by the African wind, so that those serpents harm not by their bite while alive nor by their stench when dead. I could speak of the usefulness of the ichneumons, of the crocodiles, of the cats, but I do not wish to be long. I will conclude, then, thus: that beasts have been consecrated by the barbarians for a benefit, but that of your gods not only is there no benefit forthcoming, but not even any deed at all.

Next, the air, neighbour to the sea, is distinguished into day and night; and it, now diffused and rarefied, is borne aloft, now, condensed, is gathered into clouds, and, collecting moisture, increases the earth with showers; now, flowing this way and that, makes the winds. It also makes the yearly variations of cold and heat; the same sustains the flights of birds, and, drawn in by the breath, nourishes and sustains living creatures. There remains the last and, from our dwellings, the highest embrace of the sky, girding and confining all things, which is also called ether, the outermost border and bound of the world, in which the fiery shapes mark out their ordered courses with the greatest wonder.

"He has," he says, "no business." Truly Epicurus, like some pampered child, thinks nothing better than idleness. Yet boys themselves, even when they idle, take delight in some sport or game: do we wish god to lie thus benumbed in holiday idleness, so that, if he stir himself, we should fear he cannot be blessed? This doctrine not only strips the gods of motion and divine activity, but also makes men slothful, since not even a god can be blessed if he is doing anything.

Among which the sun, by whose magnitude the earth is many times surpassed, revolves about that very earth, and, rising and setting, makes day and night; and, now approaching, now retiring, makes two reversals in each year, the one opposite to the other, from the extreme points, in the interval of which it now contracts the earth as with a kind of sadness, now in turn gladdens it, so that it seems made joyful along with the sky.

But let it be granted, as you wish, that god is the likeness and image of man: what is his dwelling, what his seat, what his place; what, next, the action of his life, by what things he is, as you would have it, blessed? For he who is to be blessed must use and enjoy his own goods. As for place, even those natures which are without souls have each its own proper place — so that earth holds the lowest, water floods over this, the air the region above, and the highest tracts are given to the ethereal fires; while of living creatures some are of the land, some of the water, some, as it were, amphibious, living in either abode; and there are some thought to be born in fire, and they often appear flitting in burning furnaces.

The moon, moreover, which is, as the mathematicians show, larger than half the earth, ranges through the same spaces as the sun, but, now meeting the sun, now parting from it, both sends to the earth that light which it has received from the sun, and itself has various changes of light; and at one time, set under and opposite to the sun, it obscures its rays and light, at another, itself falling into the shadow of the earth, when it is in the region opposite the sun, by the interposition and intervention of the earth suddenly fails. And through the same spaces those stars which we call wandering are borne about the earth, and in the same way rise and set, whose motions are now quickened, now slackened,

I ask, then, of your god, first, where he dwells; next, what cause moves him from his place, if indeed he ever moves; then, since it is proper to living things to desire something fitted to their nature, what your god desires; for what purpose, finally, he uses the motion of mind and reason; lastly, how he is blessed, how eternal. For whichever of these you touch is a sore: a doctrine so ill founded cannot find an outlet.

and often even stand still — than which spectacle nothing can be more wonderful, nothing more beautiful. There follows the very great multitude of the fixed stars, whose distinctness is so marked out that, from the likeness of known figures, they have found their names." And at this point, looking at me, he said: "I will use the verses of Aratus, which, translated by you when quite a young man, delight me so, because they are Latin, that I hold many of them in memory. So, as we see continually with our eyes, the rest of the heavenly bodies glide on, without any change or variety, with swift motion, and along with the sky are borne onward, by night and by day;

For you said that the appearance of god is perceived by thought, not by sense; that it has no solidity in it, nor abides as one in number; and that its vision is such as to be discerned by likeness and passage, and that the accession of like things from the infinite bodies never fails, and that from this it comes about that our mind, fixed upon these, deems that nature blessed and everlasting. This — by the very gods of whom we speak — what kind of thing is it after all? For if they avail only for thought and have no solidity nor prominence, what difference is there whether we think of a hippocentaur or of a god? For every such shaping of the mind the other philosophers call an empty motion, but you call it the arrival and entrance of images into our minds.

in the contemplation of which the mind of one who desires to behold the constancy of Nature can never be filled. And the uttermost point, from a double hinge, is said to be the pole.' About this are borne the two Bears, never setting; of which one is called by the Greeks Cynosura, the other is said to be Helice, whose brightest stars we behold all night long, which our people are wont to call the Seven Plough-oxen (Triones);

Thus, when I seem to see Tiberius Gracchus haranguing on the Capitol and bringing forward the voting-urn against Marcus Octavius, I call that an empty motion of the mind; but you say that the images of Gracchus and Octavius remain, which, when they have reached the Capitol, are then referred to my mind — and that the same happens with god, by whose frequent appearance our minds are struck, whence the gods are understood to be blessed and eternal.

and with stars equal and marked out alike the little Cynosura traverses the same pole of the sky. In her the Phoenicians trust as their guide on the deep at night. But the former shines forth more marked with stars, and is seen widely and at once at the first coming of night. This indeed is small, but to sailors there is use in it; for it turns in a brief and inner circle. And, that the aspect of these stars may be the more wonderful, between them, like a river with a rapid flood, the grim Dragon glides, winding itself below and above and making coils bent out of its body.

Grant that there are images by which our minds are struck: still, only a kind of appearance is presented; is there any reason why it should be blessed, why eternal? But these images of yours — what are they, and whence? This licence comes wholly from Democritus; but he too was censured by many, nor do you find a way out, and the whole matter wavers and limps. For what is less to be approved than that the images of all men fall upon me — Homer, Archilochus, Romulus, Numa, Pythagoras, Plato — and not in the form they had: how, then, were they? And of whom are these images: Aristotle teaches that the poet Orpheus never existed, and the Pythagoreans say that this Orphic poem was the work of a certain Cercon; yet Orpheus — that is, his image, as you would have it — often runs into my mind.

And while its whole shape is splendid, yet above all are to be looked upon the figure of its head and the fire of its eyes: for it not a single star alone that gleams adorning its head, but its temples are marked with a double brightness, and from its fierce eyes two glowing lights flash, and its chin shines with one radiant star; its head is bent aslant, but turned back on its rounded neck, so that you would say it fixed its gaze upon the tail of the Greater Bear.

And what of the fact that different images of the same man fall upon mine, others upon yours? What of those things that never existed at all and could not exist, such as Scylla, or the Chimaera? What of men, places, and cities that we have never seen? What of the fact that the moment I please, the image is at hand? What of the fact that they come even uninvited to a sleeping man? The whole matter, Velleius, is a trifle. Yet you cram images not only into our eyes but even into our minds: such is the impunity of prattling. And how loosely you talk!

And the rest of the Dragon's body we behold all night long; this its head here a little, and suddenly, hides itself, where rising and setting are mingled in one quarter. And touching this head there turns, as it were the image of one weary and mourning, which the Greeks are wont to call Engonasin (the Kneeler), because it is borne propped on its knees. Here is placed, with surpassing brightness, that Crown. And these things indeed are behind; but near the head is the Serpent-holder, whom the Greeks call by the famous name Ophiuchus.

"A passage of streaming visions takes place frequently, so that out of many one is seen." I should be ashamed to say I do not understand, if you yourselves who defend these things understood them. For how do you prove that the images are borne continuously, or, if continuously, how eternally? "The innumerability of atoms," he says, "supplies it." Will then this same innumerability make all things everlasting? You take refuge in equilibrium (for so let us call isonomia, if you please) and say that, since there is a mortal nature, there must also be an immortal one. In that way, since men are mortal, let there be some immortal men, and since they are born on land, let them be born in water too. "And because there are things that destroy, let there be things that preserve." Let there be, by all means; but let them preserve things that exist; that those gods of yours exist I do not perceive.

Yet how does all that semblance of things arise out of indivisible bodies? Which, even if they existed — and they do not — might perhaps push and stir one another by their concourse, but could not form, fashion, colour, or animate. In no way, then, do you produce an immortal god. Let us now look to the blessed. Without virtue, certainly, in no way; but virtue is active; and your god does nothing; he is therefore without virtue;

for beneath the breast of this Bootes is seen a star sparkling with its rays, Arcturus by famous name; beneath whose feet is borne the bright Virgin, holding the gleaming Ear of Corn in her shining body. And the signs are so measured out that in such great arrangements divine skill appears: you would have seen the twin-born Sons beneath the head of the Bear; the Crab is set beneath, in the middle, and by the feet is held the great Lion, shaking the quivering flame from his body. The Charioteer is borne beneath the left part of the Twins, drawn over against it; the fierce countenance of Helice looks upon his head. But the bright Goat holds his left shoulder. Then what follows: but this is endowed with a great and brilliant sign, while over against it the Kids cast a slender fire to mortals. Beneath whose feet the horned Bull is set, straining with his strong body. His head is sprinkled with thronging stars;

and so not even blessed. What life, then, is his? "A supply," you say, "of goods with no intervention of evils." Of what goods, pray? Of pleasures, I suppose — those, of course, that belong to the body; for you have known no pleasure of the mind that does not set out from the body and return to the body. I do not suppose you wish to be like the rest of the Epicureans, who are ashamed of certain sayings of Epicurus, in which he testifies that he cannot even understand any good that is severed from delicate and obscene pleasures — which indeed, without blushing, he pursues all of them by name.

these stars the Greeks are wont to call Hyades, from raining (for hyein in Greek is to rain), but our people unskilfully the Little Pigs (Suculae), as though they were named from pigs (sues), not from showers (imbres). And the Lesser Bear, Cepheus follows behind with outspread palms; for he turns at the very back of the Bear, the Cynosura. Him there goes before, of dim aspect of stars, Cassiopeia. And near her, with brilliant body, moves Andromeda, fleeing the mournful gaze of her parent. To her that Horse, shaking his mane with sparkling brightness, touches the top of her head with his belly, and one star, joining them, holds the two shapes with a common light, desiring to bind an everlasting knot from the stars. Next clings the Ram with twisted horns; near whom the Fishes, of which one glides on a little in front and is more touched by the bristling breezes of the north wind.

What food, then, or what drinks, or what varieties of sounds or flowers, what touches, what scents will you set before the gods to flood them with pleasures? The poets, indeed, provide nectar, ambrosia, banquets, and Youth or Ganymede to serve the cups; but you, Epicurus, what will you do? For I do not see whence your god is to have these things, nor how he is to use them. The nature of men, then, is richer for living blessedly than that of the gods, since it enjoys more kinds of pleasures.

At the feet of Andromeda Perseus is figured, whom from the highest region of the north the blasts beat. Near his left knee you will see the Pleiades (Vergiliae) with faint light. Thence the Lyre (Fides) is seen, lightly set and curved. Thence is the winged Bird beneath the broad covering of the sky. And nearest to the head of the Horse is the right hand of Aquarius, and then the whole Aquarius in succession. Then, breathing chill cold from its strong breast, half-beast in body, the Goat (Capricorn) in his great circle; whom, when the Sun has clothed him with perpetual light, bending his car at the wintry season, he wheels round.

But you reckon these the lighter pleasures, those by which, as it were, a tickling (for this is Epicurus's word) is applied to the senses. How far will you carry your jesting? For even our Philo could not endure that the Epicureans should make light of soft and delicate pleasures. For with the greatest memory he used to recite very many of Epicurus's maxims in the very words in which they were written. And of Metrodorus, who is Epicurus's colleague in wisdom, he used to quote many things still more shameless; for Metrodorus accuses his brother Timocrates, because he hesitates to measure all that pertains to the blessed life by the belly — and he says this not once but often. I see you nodding, for these things are known to you; I would produce the books if you denied it. Nor do I now blame you for referring all things to pleasure (that is another question), but I show that your gods are without pleasure, and so, by your own judgement, not even blessed. "But they are free from pain."

Here is beheld, showing himself, emerging on high, the Scorpion, drawing back behind him with the force of his body the bent Bow. Near whom, gleaming on its wings, the Bird wheels itself. But near it the Eagle bears itself with glowing body. Then the Dolphin. Thence Orion, straining with his slanting body.

Is that enough for that life most blessed and abounding in goods? "He thinks," they say, "continually that he is blessed; for he has nothing else to busy his mind with." Grasp, then, with your mind and set before your eyes a god thinking nothing else through all eternity but "it is well with me" and "I am blessed." Nor yet do I see how this blessed god of yours does not fear that he will perish, since without any pause he is struck and stirred by the everlasting onset of atoms, and since images are forever streaming off from him. So your god is neither blessed nor eternal.

Whom following, that fiery Dog shines with the light of its stars. After it the Hare follows, ceasing its course never with weary body. But at the Dog's tail the Argo glides serpent-wise. This the Ram covers, and with scaly body the Fishes, touching with its shining body the banks of the River; which you will see winding far and streaming, and the long Bonds you will behold, which hold the Fishes, set at the part of their tails. Then, near the gleaming sting of the Scorpion, you will discern the Altar, which the breath of the south wind caresses with its breeze. Near which the Centaur withdraws, hastening to join the parts of the Horse to the Claws. He, reaching out his right hand, by which the vast four-footed beast is held, stretches forth and fierce withdraws toward the bright Altar. Here from the lower parts the Hydra rears itself, whose body is spread far, and in the midst of its fold the gleaming Bowl shines. The Raven at the end, straining with feathered body, pecks with its beak; and here, beneath the very Twins, is that one Before the Dog, Procyon, which is borne under its Greek name.

"But Epicurus actually wrote books on holiness and on piety toward the gods." But in what manner does he speak in them? So that you would say you were listening to Tiberius Coruncanius or Publius Scaevola, chief pontiffs, not to a man who has utterly done away with all religion and overthrown the temples and altars of the immortal gods, not with hands, like Xerxes, but with arguments. For what reason is there for you to say that the gods are to be worshipped by men, when the gods not only do not regard men but care for nothing at all and do nothing?

Can this whole arrangement of the heavenly bodies, and this so great adornment of the sky, seem to any man of sound mind to have been able to come about from bodies coursing this way and that by chance and at random; or could any other nature, void of mind and reason, have produced these things, which not only needed reason that they might come to be, but cannot even be understood, of what kind they are, without the highest reason? Nor indeed are these things alone wonderful, but nothing is greater than that the world is so stable and so coheres for enduring that nothing fitter can even be conceived. For all its parts, everywhere pressing toward the middle place, strain equally. And bodies joined together remain longest when they are bound as by a kind of encircling chain; which is done by that nature which, achieving all things by mind and reason, is poured through the whole world, and snatches all to the middle and turns the extremes inward.

"But theirs is a certain pre-eminent and surpassing nature, such as ought of itself to draw the wise man to worship it." Can there be anything pre-eminent in a nature which, rejoicing in its own pleasure, is never going to do anything, nor does, nor has done? Moreover, what piety is owed to one from whom you have received nothing, or how can anything at all be owed to one who has done no service? For piety is justice toward the gods; but what claim of right can there be between us and them, when there is no fellowship of man with god? And holiness is the science of worshipping the gods; but why they are to be worshipped I do not understand, when no good is either received from them or hoped for.

Wherefore, if the world is globular, and for that cause all its parts everywhere even are held together both by themselves and among themselves, the same must of necessity befall the earth, so that, all its parts tending toward the middle (and that middle is the lowest point in a sphere), there is nothing to break in by which so great a tension of gravity and of weights could be made to give way. And by the same reasoning the sea, though it is above the earth, yet, seeking the middle place of the earth, is gathered into a globe evenly on every side, and never overflows nor is poured out.

And what reason is there to revere the gods out of admiration for a nature in which we see nothing excellent? For from superstition, of being freed from which you are wont to boast, it is easy to be free when you have done away with all the power of the gods. Unless perhaps you think that Diagoras, or Theodorus, who denied the gods altogether, could have been superstitious; I should not think even Protagoras, who was free to say neither that the gods exist nor that they do not. For the opinions of all these not only do away with superstition, in which there is an empty fear of the gods, but also with religion, which consists in the pious worship of the gods.

And the air, continuous with this, is borne aloft indeed by its lightness, but yet pours itself into all parts; and so it is both continued and joined with the sea, and by nature is borne to the sky, by whose thinness and heat tempered, it furnishes a vital and wholesome breath to living creatures. Embracing this, the highest part of the sky, which is called ethereal, both retains its own heat, thin and condensed by no admixture, and is joined with the outermost border of the air. And in the ether the stars are rolled, which both hold themselves gathered into globes by their own effort, and sustain their poise by their very form and figure; for they are round, by which forms, as I think I said before, they can least be harmed.

And those who said that the whole belief in the immortal gods was invented by wise men for the sake of the commonwealth, that those whom reason could not lead might be led to duty by religion — did they not utterly do away with all religion? And Prodicus of Ceos, who said that the things which were of use to the life of men had been reckoned among the gods — what religion, pray, did he leave?

Now the stars are by nature flaming; wherefore they are fed by the vapours of the earth, the sea, and the other waters, which are raised by the sun from the warmed fields and from the waters; by which the stars, fed and renewed, and all the ether, pour forth the same and again draw it back from the same source, so that almost nothing perishes, or only a very little, which the fire of the stars and the flame of the ether consume. From which our school thinks that will come to pass about which they used to say Panaetius was in doubt — that at the last the whole world will catch fire, when the moisture is consumed and neither can the earth be nourished nor the air return, whose origin could not be, all the water being drained away: so that nothing is left but fire, by which, being itself animate and a god, the world is renewed and the same adornment arises again.

And those who hand down that brave, or famous, or powerful men have after death come to be gods, and that these are the very ones whom we are wont to worship, pray to, and revere — are they not devoid of all religion? This theory was handled chiefly by Euhemerus, whom our Ennius above all others both translated and followed; but Euhemerus sets forth the deaths and the burials of the gods: does he, then, seem to have confirmed religion, or to have utterly done away with the whole of it? I pass over Eleusis, that holy and august shrine, "where the nations at the world's edge are initiated"; I leave aside Samothrace and those mysteries of Lemnos, "approached by night, in secret worship, thick-set with woodland hedges" — which, when unfolded and brought back to a rational account, teach us rather the nature of things than the nature of the gods.

I do not wish to seem to you long-winded about the reasoning of the stars, and most of all of those which are said to wander; whose great concert from most unlike motions is such that, while the highest, Saturn's, chills, the middle, Mars's, sets on fire, and Jupiter's, set between them, lights up and tempers, and below Mars two obey the sun, the sun itself fills all the world with its light, and the moon, lighted by it, brings on pregnancies and births and the ripenings of generation. Whom this coupling of things, and this consenting, as it were, fitting-together of Nature for the safety of the world, does not move, that man, I am sure, has never reflected on any of these things.

Come, that we may pass from heavenly to earthly things, what is there in these in which the reasoning of an intelligent Nature does not appear? First, of the things that are born from the earth, the stems both give stability to the things they sustain, and draw from the earth the sap by which the things held in their roots are nourished; and the trunks are clothed with bark or rind, that they may be the safer from cold and heat. Now the vines so grasp their props with their tendrils, as it were with hands, and so raise themselves up, like living creatures; nay, they are even said to flee, as from things harmful and noxious, from the stalks of the cabbage, if it has been planted near, and not to touch them in any part.

To me indeed even Democritus, a man great above all others, from whose springs Epicurus watered his little gardens, seems to waver on the nature of the gods. For at one time he holds that images endowed with divinity reside in the universe of things; at another, that the principles of mind which are in that same universe are gods; at another, that animate images, which are wont either to do us good or to harm us, are gods; at another, certain images so vast and so great as to embrace the whole world from without. All which are worthier of the fatherland of Democritus than of Democritus himself; for who can grasp those images in his mind, who admire them, who judge them worthy of worship or of religion? Epicurus, however, has plucked up religion by the roots from the minds of men, since he has done away with both the help and the favour of the immortal gods. For while he says that the nature of god is best and most excellent, he denies at the same time that there is favour in god: he takes away that which is most proper to a nature best and most excellent. For what is better or what more excellent than goodness and beneficence? And since you would have god lack this, you would have no one — neither god nor man — dear to god, no one loved by him, no one cherished: so it comes about that not only are men neglected by the gods, but the gods themselves, one by another. How much better the Stoics, who are blamed by you! For they hold that the wise are friends to the wise even though unknown to one another; for nothing is more lovable than virtue, and he who has attained it, wherever in the world he is, will be loved by us.

And how great is the variety of living creatures, how great in each a force to abide in its own kind! Of which some are covered with hides, some clothed with shaggy hair, some bristling with spines; some we see covered with feathers, some with scales, some armed with horns, some having the refuge of wings. But Nature has provided abundantly and copiously the food fitted for each living creature. I could enumerate, for the taking and consuming of that food, what skill there is in the shapes of living creatures, and how cunning and subtle the arrangement of their parts, and how wonderful the framing of their limbs. For all things which are enclosed within are so born and so placed that none of them is superfluous, none not necessary for the maintaining of life.

But you — what mischief you do, when you set kindness and goodwill in weakness! For, to say nothing of the power and nature of the gods, do you not hold that not even men, unless they were weak, would have been beneficent and kind? Is there no natural affection among the good? The very word "dear" belongs to love, from which the name of friendship is derived; and if we refer it to our own profit, not to the advantage of him whom we love, that will be no friendship but a kind of trafficking in our own interests. Meadows and fields and herds of cattle are loved in that fashion, because profit is got from them; but the affection and friendship of men is freely given. How much more, then, that of the gods, who, needing nothing, both love one another and take thought for men! And if it were not so, why do we revere and pray to the gods, why do pontiffs preside over rites and augurs over auspices, what do we ask of the immortal gods, what do we vow? "But there is even a book of Epicurus on holiness."

The same Nature, moreover, gave to the beasts both sensation and appetite, that by the one they might have an impulse to take their natural food, by the other might separate the harmful from the wholesome. Now some animals come to their food by walking, some by creeping, some by flying, some by swimming, and they take their food partly by the gape of the mouth and the very teeth, partly seize it by the gripping of claws, partly by the hookedness of their beaks; some suck, some crop, some devour, some chew. And again, some are of such lowness that they easily reach earthly food with their snouts; but those which are taller, as geese, swans, cranes, camels, are helped by the length of their necks;

We are mocked by a man not so much witty as free in the licence of his writing. For what holiness can there be if the gods take no care for human things, and what nature is there that, being animate, cares for nothing? Truer, then, no doubt, is that which Posidonius, the familiar friend of us all, set forth in the fifth book of his work On the Nature of the Gods: that Epicurus thinks there are no gods, and that what he said about the immortal gods he said to avert odium from himself; for he could not have been so senseless as to fashion a god like a little man — only in the outermost outlines, not in solid frame, endowed with all the limbs of a man yet without the least use of those limbs, a thin and transparent thing, granting nothing to anyone, doing no favour, caring for nothing at all, doing nothing. Such a nature, first, cannot exist; and Epicurus, seeing this, in fact does away with the gods while in word he leaves them;

a hand too has been given to the elephant, because, on account of the greatness of its body, it had difficult approaches to its food. But to those beasts whose food was such that they must feed on the flesh of other kinds, Nature gave either strength or swiftness. To some, too, a kind of contrivance and skill has been given, as among the little spiders some weave, as it were, a net, that they may dispatch whatever has stuck in it, while others watch, as it were, from an unexpected place, and, if anything falls in, seize it and consume it. But the pina (for so it is called in Greek), opening with two great shells, enters into a kind of partnership with a little shrimp for procuring food; and so, when little fishes have swum into the gaping shell, the pina, warned by the shrimp, closes the shells with a snap: thus by most unlike little creatures food is sought in common;

and next, if god is most certainly such that he is held by no favour and no love of men, then farewell to him — for why should I say "may he be propitious"? For he can be propitious to no one, since, as you say, all favour and love are bound up with weakness.'"

wherein it is to be wondered whether they have come together by some meeting with one another, or have been associated by Nature herself from their very birth. There is also no little wonder concerning those water-creatures which are born on land; such as the crocodiles, the river-tortoises, and certain serpents, which, born away from the water, as soon as they are first able to crawl, make for the water. Nay, we often set ducks' eggs under hens; from which the chicks, hatched, are at first nourished by them as by mothers, by which they were hatched and warmed, but then leave them and flee from them when they follow, as soon as ever they could see the water as it were their natural home: so great a guard for preserving itself has Nature implanted in living creatures. I have read it written too, that there is a certain bird called the spoonbill (platalea), which seeks its food by flying upon those birds which dive into the sea, and, when they have emerged and caught a fish, presses their heads with its bite until they let go their catch, upon which it itself pounces. And it is written too that this same bird is wont to fill itself with shellfish, and, when it has digested these by the heat of its stomach, to vomit them up, and so to pick out from them those parts that are edible.

The sea-frogs, again, are said to be wont to cover themselves with sand and to move near the water, toward which the fishes, as toward food, when they have approached, are dispatched and consumed by the frogs. The kite has a kind of natural war, as it were, with the raven; and so each, wherever it has come upon them, breaks the other's eggs. But that thing (noticed by Aristotle, by whom most things were noticed) — who can fail to wonder at it: that the cranes, when, seeking warmer regions, they cross the seas, make the form of a triangle? And by the foremost angle of this the opposing air is driven back from them, then by little and little, on either side, as by oars, so by their wings the course of the birds is lightened; but the base of the triangle which the cranes make is helped, as it were from the stern, by the winds; and they rest their necks and heads on the backs of those flying before them; and because the leader himself cannot do this, since he has nothing to rest on, he flies back that he too may rest, and into his place comes one of those that have rested, and this interchange is kept up throughout the whole flight.

Many things of this kind I could bring forward, but you see the general sort. Now those things too are better known — how greatly the beasts guard themselves, how they look about in feeding, how they hide in their lairs. And those things are wonderful, that — the very things which lately, that is, a few ages ago, were discovered by the genius of physicians — the dogs cure themselves by vomiting, but the Egyptian ibises by purging the bowels. It has been heard that the panthers, which in barbarous lands are caught by poisoned flesh, have a certain remedy, which, when they have used it, they do not die; and that the wild goats in Crete, when they have been pierced by poisoned arrows, seek an herb which is called dittany, which, when they have tasted, they say the arrows fall out of their bodies;

and that the hinds, a little before bringing forth, thoroughly purge themselves with a certain herb which is called seselis. Now those things we behold — how each defends itself with its own weapons against violence and fear: the bulls with their horns, the boars with their tusks, the lions by running; some protect themselves by flight, some by hiding, the cuttlefish by pouring forth ink, the torpedo-fish by numbing, and many drive off their pursuers by the intolerable foulness of their smell. But that the adornment of the world might be perpetual, great care was taken by the providence of the gods that there should always be both kinds of beasts and trees and all the things which are held in the earth by their stems; all which indeed have in themselves that force of seed that from one many are generated. And that seed is enclosed in the inmost part of those berries which are poured forth from each plant, and by the same seeds both men are fed abundantly and the earth is filled with the renewal of plants of the same kind.

Why should I tell how great a design appears in the beasts for the perpetual preservation of their kind? For first, some are male, some female, which Nature contrived for the sake of perpetuity; next, the parts of the body are most apt both for procreating and for conceiving, and in male and female there are wonderful desires for the mingling of their bodies; and when the seed has settled in its place, it draws to itself almost all the nourishment and, walled in by it, fashions the living creature; which, when it has slipped from the womb and fallen out, in those creatures which are nourished by milk almost all the food of the mothers begins to turn to milk, and the things which have just been born, without a teacher, by the guidance of Nature, seek the teats and are filled with their abundance. And, that we may understand that none of these things is fortuitous, and that all these are the works of a provident and skilful Nature, those creatures which bring forth manifold offspring, as the sows, as the dogs, have been given a multitude of teats, which same teats those beasts have few which bring forth few.

Why should I tell how great is the love of beasts in rearing and guarding the things they have begotten, even to that limit at which they can defend themselves? Although the fishes, as they say, when they have produced their eggs, leave them, for those eggs are easily both sustained by the water and bring forth the brood; but tortoises and crocodiles, they say, when they have laid their eggs on land, bury them and then go away: so the young are both born and reared of themselves. Now hens and the rest of the birds both seek a quiet place for laying, and build themselves beds and nests, and strew these as soft as they can, that the eggs may be most easily preserved; and when they have hatched out their chicks from these, they so watch over them that they both warm them with their wings, lest they be hurt by the cold, and, if there is heat from the sun, set themselves against it; but when the chicks can use their little wings, then the mothers attend their flights and are freed from the rest of their care.

There is added, too, for the preservation and safety of some living creatures and of those things which the earth produces, the skill and diligence of men. For there are many both flocks and plants which cannot be safe without the care of men. Great opportunities, too, for the tillage and abundance of men are found in different places. The Nile waters Egypt, and, when it has held it through the whole summer overwhelmed and covered, then retires and leaves the fields, softened and silted, for sowing. The Euphrates makes Mesopotamia fertile, into which it carries every year, as it were, new fields. The Indus, indeed, which is the greatest of all rivers, not only gladdens and softens the fields with its water, but even sows them; for it is said to carry down with it a great quantity of seeds like grain.

And I could bring forward many other memorable things in other places, many fields fertile, some of one kind of fruit, some of another. But how great is the kindness of Nature, in that it brings forth so many things for food, so varied, so pleasant, and these not at one season of the year, so that we are always delighted both by novelty and by abundance! How seasonable, too, how wholesome, not only to the race of men but also to that of cattle, and in short to all things that arise from the earth, are the Etesian winds which she has given; by whose blowing excessive heats are tempered, and by the same the swift and sure courses of the sea are directed! Many things must be passed over, and yet many are told.

For there cannot be enumerated the conveniences of rivers, the tides of the sea ever advancing and retreating, the mountains clothed and wooded, the salt-pans far removed from the seashore, the lands most full of wholesome medicines, and finally the innumerable arts necessary for sustenance and for life. Now the alternation of day and night preserves living creatures, granting one time for acting, another for resting. Thus on every side, by every reasoning, it is concluded that all things in this world are administered wonderfully by a divine mind and counsel for the welfare and preservation of all.

But if anyone shall ask for whose sake so great a construction of things was made — was it for the trees and herbs, which, though without sensation, are yet sustained by Nature? But that indeed is absurd. Or for the beasts? It is no whit more probable that the gods toiled so greatly for the sake of dumb things that understand nothing. For whose sake, then, would one say the world was made? Doubtless for the sake of those living creatures which use reason; these are gods and men, than whom assuredly nothing is better, for it is reason which excels all things. So it becomes credible that the world, and all the things that are in that world, were made for the sake of gods and men. And it will the more easily be understood that the immortal gods have provided for men, if the whole framing of man is surveyed, and all the figure and perfection of human nature.

For since the life of living creatures is held by three things — food, drink, breath — for the taking in of all these the mouth is best fitted, which, with the nostrils joined to it, is increased by the breath, while by the teeth set in the mouth the food is chewed and by them made small and soft. The front ones, sharp, divide the food by biting, but the inmost, which are called the grinders (genuini), reduce it; which reducing seems to be helped also by the tongue.

The tongue, then, the gullet, clinging to its roots, receives, into which first slide down the things which have been taken in by the mouth. It, touching the tonsils on either side, is bounded by the outermost and inmost part of the palate, and, when by the working and motions of the tongue it has received the food thrust down and as it were forced upon it, drives it downward. And those parts of it which are below that which is swallowed are dilated, while those above are contracted.

But since the rough windpipe (for so it is called by the physicians) has its opening joined to the roots of the tongue a little above where the gullet is fastened to the tongue, and reaches as far as the lungs and receives the air which is drawn in by the breath, and breathes the same out again from the lungs and gives it back, it is covered by a kind of lid, which was given for this cause, that, if any food should by chance fall into it, the breath might not be hindered. But since the belly, set beneath the gullet, is the receptacle of food and drink, while the lungs and heart draw in breath from without, in the belly many things are wonderfully effected, which consist for the most part of fibres; and it is manifold and winding, and confines and holds whatever it has received, whether dry or moist, that it may be changed and digested, and it is now drawn tight, now relaxed, and forces and confounds all that it has received, so that easily, both by the heat which it has in plenty, and by the grinding of the food, and besides by the breath, all things, cooked and prepared, are distributed to the rest of the body. In the lungs, moreover, there is a certain rareness and a softness like to sponges, very apt for drawing in the breath, which now contract themselves in breathing in, now are dilated by breathing out, that the food of the air may be drawn in frequently, by which living creatures are chiefly nourished.

From the intestines, moreover, the juice by which we are nourished, separated from the rest of the food, flows through to the liver by certain ways drawn and directed from the middle intestine even to what are called the 'gates' of the liver, which reach to the liver and cling to it; and from there other channels [run on], through which falls the food that has slipped down from the liver. From that food, when the bile has been separated, and the humours which are poured forth from the kidneys, the rest turns itself into blood and flows together to those same gates of the liver, to which all its ways lead; through which the food, slipping down, is in this very place poured into that vein which is called the hollow vein (cava), and through it, now prepared and digested, glides to the heart; and from the heart it is distributed into the whole body through very many veins reaching into all parts of the body.

But in what manner the leavings of the food are driven off, the intestines now drawing themselves tight, now relaxing, it is not at all hard to say, but yet it must be passed over, lest the discourse should have anything of unpleasantness. Let rather that incredible workmanship of Nature be unfolded: for the air which is drawn into the lungs by the breath grows warm, first by the breath itself, then by the contact of the lungs, and of it part is given back in breathing out, part is received by a certain part of the heart which is called the ventricle of the heart, to which another like it is joined, into which the blood flows from the liver through that hollow vein. And in that way, from those parts, both the blood is diffused through the veins into the whole body and the breath through the arteries; and both, frequent and many, interwoven through the whole body, bear witness to a certain incredible force of skilful and divine workmanship.

Why should I speak of the bones, which, set beneath the body, have wonderful joints, both fitted for stability, and suited for limiting the limbs, and apt for motion and for every action of the body? Add to this the sinews, by which the limbs are held together, and their interlacing reaching through the whole body, which, like the veins and arteries, drawn and set out from the heart, are led into the whole body.

To this providence of Nature, so diligent and so skilful, many things can be added, from which it may be understood how great and how surpassing are the gifts bestowed on men by the gods. Who first set men upright, raised from the ground, lofty and erect, that, gazing at the sky, they might be able to attain the knowledge of the gods. For men are sprung from the earth not as dwellers and inhabitants but as it were spectators of the things above and the heavenly, the spectacle of which belongs to no other kind of living creature. The senses, moreover, the interpreters and messengers of things, are wonderfully made and placed in the head as in a citadel, for their necessary uses. For the eyes, as scouts, hold the highest place, from which, beholding most things, they perform their office;

and the ears, since they must perceive sound, which by nature is borne aloft, are rightly placed in the high parts of the body; and likewise the nostrils, because every smell is borne upward, are rightly above, and, because their judgement of food and drink is great, not without cause have followed the neighbourhood of the mouth. Now taste, which should perceive the kinds of the things we feed on, dwells in that part of the mouth by which Nature has opened a way for things eaten and drunk. But touch is spread evenly over the whole body, that we may be able to feel all blows and all too violent assaults of cold and heat. And as in buildings the architects turn away from the eyes and noses of the masters those things which, flowing off, must needs have something foul, so Nature has banished like things far from the senses.

But what craftsman besides Nature, than whom nothing can be more cunning, could have pursued so great a skill in the senses? Who first clothed and fenced the eyes with the thinnest membranes; which first she made translucent, that one might see through them, but firm, that they might be held together. But she made the eyes slippery and mobile, both that they might turn aside if anything should harm them, and that they might easily turn their gaze where they would; and the very keen point by which we see, which is called the pupil, is so small that it easily avoids the things which might harm it; and the eyelids, which are the coverings of the eyes, most soft to the touch lest they should hurt the eyesight, were made most aptly both for closing the pupils, lest anything fall in, and for opening them; and she provided that this could be done again and again with the greatest speed.

And the eyelids are fenced as with a rampart of hairs, by which, when the eyes are open, anything that fell in might be repelled, and, when they are closed in sleep, since we needed the eyes not for seeing, they might rest as it were wrapped up. Besides, they are usefully hidden and fenced on every side by lofty parts. For first the upper parts, overhung by the brows, repel the sweat flowing down from the head and forehead; the cheeks next, set beneath and slightly rising, guard from the lower part; and the nose is so placed that it seems set as a wall between the eyes.

The hearing, moreover, is always open, for we need its sense even when asleep, and when a sound has been received by it we are roused even from sleep. It has a winding passage, lest anything should be able to enter if it lay open simple and straight; and provision was made too that, if any tiny creature should try to break in, it should stick fast in the dirt of the ears as in birdlime. But on the outside project what are called the ears, both made for covering and protecting the sense, and lest the voices that strike should slip away and wander before the sense had been struck by them. But they have entrances hard and as it were horny and with many windings, because by these natures the sound carried back is amplified; wherefore in the lyre too there is resonance from the shell or from horn, and from winding and enclosed places things are echoed back more fully.

Likewise the nostrils, which, on account of necessary uses, are always open, have narrower entrances, lest anything that might harm should be able to pass into them; and they always have a moisture not useless for driving off dust and many other things. The taste is excellently fenced; for it is contained in the mouth, both aptly for use and for the keeping of safety. And all the senses of men far surpass the senses of the beasts. For first, in those arts of which the judgement belongs to the eyes — in painted, modelled, and engraved forms, and also in the motion and gesture of bodies — the eyes discern many things more subtly; and the eyes judge also the charm and order, and, so to say, the seemliness of colours and shapes; and even greater things: for they know both virtues and vices; they know the angry and the propitious, the rejoicing and the grieving, the brave and the cowardly, the bold and the timid.

And of the ears likewise there is a kind of wonderful and skilful judgement, by which is judged, in the songs of voice and pipe and string, the variety of sounds, the intervals, the distinctness, and the very many kinds of voice — tuneful and dull, smooth and rough, deep and shrill, flexible and hard — which are judged by the ears of men alone. And of the nostrils likewise, and of taste, and in part of touch, there are great judgements. And for the taking and full enjoyment of these senses, more arts even than I could wish have been discovered; for it is plain to what lengths the compoundings of perfumes, the seasonings of foods, the allurements of bodies have advanced.

Now the very mind and intellect of man, his reason, counsel, prudence — whoever does not perceive that these have been perfected by divine care, he seems to me to lack these very things. While I discuss this, I could wish that your eloquence, Cotta, were given me. For in what fashion would you set forth how great, first, is the intelligence in us, then the joining and grasping of consequences along with their first principles; from which, of course, we judge what is brought about from what causes, and conclude this by reason, and define single things and grasp them within a circumscribing bound; from which is understood what force knowledge has and of what kind it is, than which not even in god is there anything more excellent. But how great are those things which you Academics weaken and do away with — that both by the senses and by the mind we perceive and grasp the things that are outside us;

from which, compared and matched among themselves, we also form arts, some necessary for the use of life, some for delight. And again, that mistress of things, as you are wont to say, the power of speaking, how splendid it is and how divine! Which first brings it about that we can both learn the things we do not know and teach others the things we know; then by this we exhort, by this we persuade, by this we console the afflicted, by this we lead the terrified away from fear, by this we restrain the exultant, by this we quench desires and angers; this has bound us together by the fellowship of law, of statutes, of cities; this has separated us from a savage and brutish life.

And for the use of speech it is incredible, unless you attend diligently, how great works Nature has contrived. For first the windpipe reaches from the lungs to the inmost mouth, through which the voice, taking its beginning from the mind, is received and poured forth. Then in the mouth is set the tongue, bounded by the teeth; it shapes and limits the voice poured forth without measure, and makes the sounds of the voice distinct and pressed, when it strikes both the teeth and other parts of the mouth; and so our people are wont to call the tongue like a plectrum, the teeth like strings, the nostrils like the horns which resound to the strings in songs.

And how apt, and how serviceable for many arts, are the hands which Nature gave to man! For the bending of the fingers is easy, and easy their stretching, on account of the soft joints and articulations, and they labour in no motion. And so for painting, modelling, carving, for drawing forth the sounds of strings and pipes, the hand is apt by the application of the fingers. And these are matters of delight, those of necessity — I mean the tillage of fields, the building of houses, the coverings of bodies whether woven or sewn, and all the working of bronze and iron; from which it is understood that, by things discovered by the mind, perceived by the senses, with the hands of craftsmen brought to bear, we have attained all things, so that we could be housed, clothed, safe, and have cities, walls, dwellings, and shrines.

Now by the works of men, that is, by their hands, variety also and abundance of food is found. For the fields bring forth many things sought by the hand, which are either consumed at once or, stored up, are entrusted to keeping; and besides, we feed on beasts both of land and of water and of the air, partly by catching, partly by rearing. We also bring about, by our taming, the carriages of four-footed beasts, whose swiftness and strength lend strength and swiftness to ourselves. We lay burdens on some beasts, we put yokes upon them; we turn to our advantage the most acute senses of elephants and the keenness of dogs; we draw forth iron from the caverns of the earth, a thing necessary for tilling the fields; we find the deeply hidden veins of bronze, silver, and gold, both apt for use and comely for adornment. And by the felling of trees and by all timber, whether cultivated or of the woods, we use it partly for warming the body by applying fire and for softening food, partly for building, that, fenced by roofs, we may drive off cold and heat;

and it brings great use, too, for the making of ships, by whose voyages all supplies for life are furnished from every side; and the things which Nature has begotten most violent — the sea and the winds — we alone have the governing of, through our knowledge of nautical matters, and we enjoy and use very many things of the sea. And likewise of earthly advantages there is in man the whole mastery: we enjoy plains, we enjoy mountains; ours are the rivers, ours the lakes; we sow crops, we plant trees; we give fertility to the lands by leading in waters; we dam, direct, and turn aside rivers; in short, with our own hands we strive to make, in the nature of things, as it were a second nature.

And what of the reason of men — has it not penetrated even to the sky? For we alone of living creatures have come to know the risings, settings, and courses of the stars; by the race of men the day, the month, the year have been bounded; the eclipses of the sun and moon have been known and foretold for all time to come — how great they will be, and when. Contemplating which, the mind comes to the knowledge of the gods, from which arises piety, to which justice is joined and the rest of the virtues, from which springs a blessed life, equal and like to that of the gods, yielding to the heavenly ones in nothing save immortality, which has nothing to do with living well. By the setting forth of which things I seem to have sufficiently shown how far the nature of man surpasses all living creatures. From which it ought to be understood that neither the figure and position of the limbs nor the force of the genius and mind could have been brought about by fortune.

It remains for me to show, and at length to conclude, that all things which are in this world, of which men make use, were made and prepared for the sake of men. In the first place, the world itself was made for the sake of gods and men, and the things which are in it were prepared and devised for the use of men. For the world is, as it were, the common house of gods and men, or a city of both; for they alone, using reason, live by right and by law. As, then, we must hold that Athens and Lacedaemon were founded for the sake of the Athenians and Lacedaemonians, and all the things that are in those cities are rightly said to belong to those peoples, so whatever things are in the whole world must be held to belong to the gods and to men.

Now the circuits of the sun and moon and the rest of the heavenly bodies, although they pertain also to the coherence of the world, yet furnish a spectacle to men too; for there is no sight more insatiable, none more beautiful, and none more excellent for reason and skill; for, measuring their courses, we have come to know the ripenings and the varieties and changes of the seasons. And if these are known to men alone, we must judge that they were made for the sake of men.

And the earth, teeming with crops and with the various kinds of pulse, which it pours forth with the greatest bounty — does it seem to bring these forth for the sake of beasts or of men? What shall I say of the vines and the olive-groves, whose most plentiful and most joyous fruits in no way pertain to the beasts? For of sowing, of tilling, of reaping the fruits in season and gathering them in, of storing and laying them by, there is no knowledge in the cattle, and the use and care of all these things is man's.

As the lyre, then, and the pipes must be said to have been made for the sake of those who could use them, so the things I have spoken of must be confessed to have been prepared for those alone who use them; nor, if some beasts steal or snatch something of them, shall we say that they too were born for the sake of the beasts. For men do not store grain for the sake of mice and ants, but for the sake of their wives, children, and households; so the beasts, as I said, enjoy it by stealth, the masters openly and freely;

it must be confessed, then, that these stores of things were procured for the sake of men. Unless perhaps the great abundance and variety of fruits, and their pleasantness not only of taste but also of smell and sight, brings any doubt that Nature has given them to men alone. And so far is it from being true that these things were prepared even for the sake of the beasts, that we see the very beasts begotten for the sake of men. For what else do the sheep furnish but that, their fleeces being dressed and woven, men may be clothed? — sheep which indeed could neither be fed nor sustained nor yield any fruit from themselves without the tillage and care of men. And the so faithful guarding of dogs, their so loving fawning upon their masters, their so great hatred of strangers, and their so incredible keenness of nose for tracking, their so great eagerness in hunting — what else does it mean but that they were begotten for the conveniences of men?

Why should I speak of oxen? Whose very backs declare that they were not shaped for receiving a burden, but their necks born for the yoke, and the strength and breadth of their shoulders for drawing ploughs. By which, when the lands were broken up by the cleaving of clods, by that golden race, as the poets say, no violence was ever done them; but then the iron race suddenly arose, and dared first to forge the deadly sword and to taste the bullock joined to the yoke and tamed by its own hand: so great a usefulness was thought to be got from oxen that to feed upon their flesh was held a crime. It would be long to follow out the uses of mules and asses, which surely were prepared for the use of men.

But the pig — what has it besides food? To which indeed Chrysippus says that its very soul was given for salt, lest it should rot; in which beast, because it was fitted for the feeding of men, Nature has begotten nothing more fruitful. What shall I say of the multitude and the sweetness of fishes, what of birds? From which so great a pleasure is got that at times our Stoic Providence seems to have been Epicurean; and these could not even be caught save by the reason and skill of men — although certain birds, both flyers and singers (as our augurs call them), we think to have been born for the sake of taking auguries.

Now the huge and wild beasts we get by hunting, both that we may feed on them and that we may exercise ourselves in hunting after the likeness of military training, and that we may use them tamed and well-broken, as the elephants, and that we may choose out of their bodies many remedies for diseases and wounds, just as from certain plants and herbs, whose usefulness we have perceived by the experience and trial of long time. One may survey with the mind, as with the eyes, the whole earth and all the seas: you will discern now the fruitful and measureless spaces of the plains, and the thickest clothing of the mountains, the pastures of cattle, then the sea-courses of incredible swiftness.

Nor indeed above the earth alone, but even in its inmost darkness, lies hidden the usefulness of very many things, which, arising for the use of men, is found by men alone. But that point, which either of you will perhaps seize on to censure — Cotta, because Carneades gladly inveighed against the Stoics; Velleius, because Epicurus mocks nothing so much as the prediction of things to come — seems to me to confirm most of all that human affairs are cared for by the prudence of the gods. For there is assuredly divination, which appears in many places, things, and times, both in private and most of all in public affairs:

the soothsayers discern many things, the augurs foresee many things; many things are declared by oracles, many by prophecies, many by dreams, many by portents; by the knowledge of which many things have often been gained according to the wish and advantage of men, and many dangers also driven off. This, then, whether it be a power, or an art, or a nature, has assuredly been given to man for the knowledge of things to come, and to no other by the immortal gods. And if these things, taken singly, perhaps do not move you, yet at least, all connected and joined together among themselves, they ought to have moved you.

Nor indeed is it for the whole race of men alone, but for individuals also, that the immortal gods are wont to take thought and provide. For we may contract the universality of the human race and bring it down step by step to fewer, and at last to single men. For if we judge that the gods take thought for all men who are anywhere, on whatever coast and part of the lands, distant from the continuity of this land which we inhabit, for the causes which we mentioned before, they take thought also for these men who, with us, dwell in these lands from east to west.

But if they take thought for those who dwell, as it were, in a kind of great island which we call the orb of the earth, they take thought also for those who hold the parts of that island, Europe, Asia, Africa. Therefore they cherish both the parts of these, as Rome, Athens, Sparta, Rhodes, and, of those cities, apart from the whole, single men, as in the war with Pyrrhus, Curius, Fabricius, Coruncanius; in the first Punic War, Calatinus, Duellius, Metellus, Lutatius; in the second, Maximus, Marcellus, Africanus; after these, Paulus, Gracchus, Cato; and in our fathers' memory, Scipio, Laelius; and many other singular men besides, both our state and Greece has borne, of whom we must believe that none was such save by the help of god.

This reasoning impelled the poets, and most of all Homer, to attach to the chief of the heroes — Ulysses, Diomedes, Agamemnon, Achilles — certain gods as companions of their crises and dangers. Besides, the frequent presences of the gods themselves, such as I recounted above, declare that the gods take thought both for states and for single men. Which indeed is understood also by the foretokens of things to come, which are portended now to the sleeping, now to the waking; besides, we are admonished by many omens, by many things in the entrails, and by many other things, which long use has so marked that it has made the art of divination.

No man, therefore, was ever great without some divine inspiration. Nor indeed must it be so refuted that, if a storm has harmed the crops or vineyards of anyone, or if chance has taken away anything from the conveniences of life, we should judge the man to whom any of these things has happened either hated by god or neglected by god. The gods care for great things, the small they neglect. But to great men all things are always prosperous, if indeed enough has been said by our school and by the chief of philosophy, Socrates, concerning the rich plenty and abundance of virtue.

These things, in the main, came into my mind which I thought ought to be said concerning the nature of the gods. But you, Cotta, if you would listen to me, would plead the same cause, and would bethink yourself that you are both a leading citizen and a pontiff, and, since it is allowed you to argue on either side, would take this side rather, and would bring to this rather that faculty of arguing which, received from your rhetorical exercises, the Academy has enlarged. For an evil and impious custom it is to argue against the gods, whether it be done in earnest or in pretence."
